Environmental and Emotional
Barriers to School Attendance
(EEBSA) is a term used to describe a
child's difficulty attending or
engaging with school due to
emotional factors. Children may
display EEBSA in a variety of ways,
and recognising the early signs can
help ensure they receive the right
support (please see the image
provided by Cambridgeshire County
Council highlighting signs of
EEBSA).

If you have concerns that your child
may be showing signs of EEBSA,
please speak to your child's class
teacher or a member of the Senior
Leadership Team. By working
together, we can develop a shared
understanding of your child's
strengths and any barriers they may
be facing, with the aim of supporting
their wellbeing and helping them feel
happy and successful at school.

Coffee Afternoon on
Wednesday 18th November from
2:30pm to 3:00pm

. Parents and carers
are warmly invited to attend to find
out more about EEBSA, discuss any
concerns, and learn about the support
available.

At our school, we are proud to
support our Young Carers and
recognise the important role they
play within their families. We work
closely with Centre 33 to provide
external support, while internally we
offer fortnightly Young Carers

take part in activities, and relax in a
supportive environment. Led by Miss
Coles and Mrs Flisher, with support
from Mr Bostock, these sessions help

understood, and supported. We are
also committed to raising awareness
across the school community and
celebrating the dedication, resilience,
and compassion shown by our Young
Carers every day.

Please follow the link below to flag

can include practical tasks, emotional
support, or helping siblings, and it
may take place before or after the
school day. We recognise that these
responsibilities can sometimes impact
a child’s wellbeing, learning, and
emotional needs. All conversations
and responses will be treated
sensitively and in confidence.

💛 Could you help keep our PTFA
going?

Our PTFA is a wonderful part of the
Warboys Primary Academy
community, helping to bring exciting
events and opportunities to our
children while raising much-needed
funds for the school. However,

we
urgently need more parents and carers
to get involved.

Following several of our valued
committee members stepping down
as their children finished at the
school last year, we are now facing a
very real challenge.

We are losing our
Treasurer, along with other
experienced members, and without
enough people willing to step forward,
we may have no choice but to fold the
PTFA.

We really don't want that to happen.
You might think you need lots of free
time or previous experience to join
the PTFA,

We need people
who can help in whatever way they
can. That could mean helping at an
event, coming along with ideas,
taking on a committee role, helping
with fundraising, or simply lending a
hand occasionally.

Every person who gets involved
makes the workload lighter for
everyone else — and helps us
continue providing those extra
experiences and opportunities
for our children.

A quick reminder that our PTFA sell
high‑quality

through their Facebook page. It’s a
great way to save money, support the
school, and give uniform items a new
life.Please check out their page if you
need any extra bits for the term

If you require any further
information or have any questions or
concerns, please don’t hesitate to get
in touch with us in the school office -
we’re here to help.

Want to learn more? Take a look
around our website at

— you’ll find
plenty of helpful information.

REMEMBER - If you feel that a child
is unsafe, then please use the
following ways to contact help.

Call Social Services on 0345 045 5203
and make a referral. This can be an
anonymous referral if this feels safer.

Call 999 IF CHILD IS IN
IMMEDIATE DANGER.

You can also use our emergency email
address
(safeguarding@wpa.education). BUT
please use the other options first, so
as not to delay help for a child.

Diwali Dance Workshop -
Voluntary Contributions Needed

announcements.title: EEBSA-Environmental and Emotional Barriers to Scho
announcements.content:
EEBSA

-Environmental

and Emotional

Barriers to

School

Attendance

Environmental and Emotional
Barriers to School Attendance
(EEBSA) is a term used to describe a
child's difficulty attending or
engaging with school due to
emotional factors. Children may
display EEBSA in a variety of ways,
and recognising the early signs can
help ensure they receive the right
support (please see the image
provided by Cambridgeshire County
Council highlighting signs of
EEBSA).

If you have concerns that your child
may be showing signs of EEBSA,
please speak to your child's class
teacher or a member of the Senior
Leadership Team. By working
together, we can develop a shared
understanding of your child's
strengths and any barriers they may
be facing, with the aim of supporting
their wellbeing and helping them feel
happy and successful at school.

Miss Westwood

will be hosting an
informal

Coffee Afternoon on
Wednesday 18th November from
2:30pm to 3:00pm

. Parents and carers
are warmly invited to attend to find
out more about EEBSA, discuss any
concerns, and learn about the support
available.

We look forward to seeing you there.

(TAPP).

98%
attendance or above

each term will be
invited to a special pizza party during

receive a raffle ticket for the chance
to win a

£50 Amazon voucher.

At Warboys Primary Academy, we
know that good attendance plays a
vital role in children's academic
achievement, social development and
wellbeing. Thank you for your
continued support in helping your
child attend school regularly and

best opportunity to thrive.

Term-time leave

can happen, and we’re always here to
support families where possible.

However, Cambridgeshire County

Non-attendance at school and the

announcements.title: Young Carers: Support & Parent Concern Form
announcements.content:
At our school, we are proud to
support our Young Carers and
recognise the important role they
play within their families. We work
closely with Centre 33 to provide
external support, while internally we
offer fortnightly Young Carers
sessions where children can come
together to chat, share experiences,
take part in activities, and relax in a
supportive environment. Led by Miss
Coles and Mrs Flisher, with support
from Mr Bostock, these sessions help
ensure our Young Carers feel valued,
understood, and supported. We are
also committed to raising awareness
across the school community and
celebrating the dedication, resilience,
and compassion shown by our Young
Carers every day.

Please follow the link below to flag
any child that you may deem to be a
Young Carer. A Young Carer is a
child young person who helps to look
after a family member who may have
an illness, disability, mental health
difficulty, or who may need extra
support for another reason. This care
can include practical tasks, emotional
support, or helping siblings, and it
may take place before or after the
school day. We recognise that these
responsibilities can sometimes impact
a child’s wellbeing, learning, and
emotional needs. All conversations
and responses will be treated
sensitively and in confidence.

announcements.title: P.T.F.A: Pre-Loved School Uniform Sales
announcements.content:
A Word from the

P.T.F.A

💛 Could you help keep our PTFA
going?

Our PTFA is a wonderful part of the
Warboys Primary Academy
community, helping to bring exciting
events and opportunities to our
children while raising much-needed
funds for the school. However,

we
urgently need more parents and carers
to get involved.

Following several of our valued
committee members stepping down
as their children finished at the
school last year, we are now facing a
very real challenge.

We are losing our
Treasurer, along with other
experienced members, and without
enough people willing to step forward,
we may have no choice but to fold the
PTFA.

We really don't want that to happen.
You might think you need lots of free
time or previous experience to join
the PTFA,

you don't!

We need people
who can help in whatever way they
can. That could mean helping at an
event, coming along with ideas,
taking on a committee role, helping
with fundraising, or simply lending a
hand occasionally.

Every person who gets involved
makes the workload lighter for
everyone else — and helps us
continue providing those extra
experiences and opportunities
for our children.

💛

Pre‑Loved School Uniform

A quick reminder that our PTFA sell
high‑quality

pre‑loved uniform

through their Facebook page. It’s a
great way to save money, support the
school, and give uniform items a new
life.Please check out their page if you
need any extra bits for the term

HERE.

Welcome to this week’s school
newsletter!

What a very busy and eventful week

announcements.title: Headteacher's Message: Welcome to this week’s school newsletter!
announcements.content:
Welcome to this week’s school
newsletter!

What a very busy and eventful week
it has been! We welcomed inspectors
into school for our two-day Ofsted
inspection, and I would like to extend
a heartfelt thank you to all of our
parents and carers who took the time
to share their feedback. Your
comments and perspectives helped
inspectors gain a truly rounded
understanding of our school
community and the experiences of
our families.

I would also like to say a huge well
done and thank you to our wonderful
pupils, who spoke so confidently and
thoughtfully about their experiences
at Warboys. They represented our
school brilliantly and should be
incredibly proud of themselves.

As we reach the end of a very full half
term, I think it is fair to say that
staff, pupils and families alike are all
feeling ready for a well-earned break.
We hope you enjoy some special
family time over the holidays,
whether that involves pumpkin
picking, autumn walks, cosy days at
home, or simply making the most of
the autumn season.

Thank you, as always, for your
continued support. We wish you all a
restful and enjoyable half term and
look forward to welcoming everyone
back for our final term of the
calendar year.

Have a wonderful half term! 🍂🎃

announcements.title: School Reminders: Inhalers, Absences & School Dinners
announcements.content:
Important News

and Reminders

🎓 Secondary School
Applications – September 2027

A reminder to

Year 6 parents and
carers

that applications for a
secondary school place for

September
2027

should be submitted online by

31 October 2026.

Key dates:

Application deadline:

31 October
2026

National Offer Day:

1 March 2027

Applications received after 31
October will be classed as

late

, with
offers made on

23 April 2027

.

Parents and carers of

twins, triplets
or other multiple births

must
complete a separate application for
each child.

Families living outside
Cambridgeshire should apply
through their

home local authority.

Information about secondary schools,
open evenings and admissions
criteria can be found on the
Cambridgeshire County Council
website.

Diwali Dance Workshop -
Voluntary Contributions Needed

We are very much looking forward to
our

Diwali Dance Workshop

taking
place on

Friday 6th November 2026

for children in

EYFS and KS1

. This
exciting experience supports our RE
curriculum and will give children the
opportunity to learn about the Hindu
Festival of Lights through
storytelling, movement and dance.

Unfortunately, at present we have
received very few voluntary
contributions towards the cost of the
workshop. As these contributions
help fund the instructor leading the
sessions, we may need to

cancel the
workshop if insufficient funds are
received.

If you would like your child to benefit
from this enriching cultural
experience, we kindly ask for a
voluntary contribution of

£5.00 per
child

where possible. Payments can
be made via

your MCAS app

, and the
payment window will remain open
until

Friday 6th November 2026.

We know the children would
thoroughly enjoy this opportunity and
we hope that, with your support, we
will be able to go ahead with the
workshops as planned. Thank you for
your continued support. 🪔✨

Parent Consultation
Appointments

We are pleased to let parents and
carers know that

Parent Consultation
appointments are now live and
available to book

These meetings provide a valuable
opportunity to discuss your child's
progress, celebrate their
achievements, and talk through any
areas where they may need
additional support. We strongly
encourage all families to book an
appointment with their child's class
teacher.

Appointments can be booked via

MCAS (My Child at School)

. Please
log in to the app and select your
preferred time slot as soon as
possible, as appointments are
allocated on a first-come, first-served
basis.

If you experience any difficulties
booking your appointment, please
contact the school office for
assistance.

School Photographs

Vancols school
photographs are now available to
view and order

using the

QR code on
your proof card.

Just a reminder for
over the holidays that the cut-off date
to order the photos with free delivery
back to the school is

Thursday 29th
October at midnight.

If you have not yet registered, don't
worry. Simply scan the QR code on
your proof card and follow the
instructions provided to access your
photographs online.

If you have not received your proof
card, or it has been misplaced, please
contact the

Vancols Parent Line on
01206 273711.

We hope you enjoy viewing this year's
school photographs!

Cost of Living Support Update

We would like to make families aware
that the

Cambridgeshire Holiday
Voucher Scheme has now ended.

While holiday vouchers are no longer
available, a range of support
continues to be offered for families
who may be experiencing financial
difficulties.

The

Crisis and Resilience Fund

has
replaced the Household Support
Fund and is available until

31 March
2029

. Eligible families may be able to
access support with essential
household costs, and families who
previously received holiday vouchers
may be prioritised where appropriate.

We also encourage eligible families to
explore the

Holiday Activities and
Food (HAF) Programme

, which
provides free holiday activities,
healthy meals and snacks for children
during school holidays.

For further information about
available support and cost of living
assistance, please visit the
Cambridgeshire County Council
website or contact the School Office,
where we will be happy to signpost
families to additional sources of help.

Year 4 Residential Visit to
Grafham Water

We are pleased to let Year 4 parents
and carers know that

deposits are
now payable via the MCAS app

for
our exciting residential visit to

Grafham Water

, taking place from

Monday 28th June to Wednesday 30th
June 2027.

To

secure your child’s place, a non-
refundable deposit of £75

is required.
Once the deposit has been paid, the

remaining balance can be paid in
monthly instalments through MCAS.

We hope that offering the opportunity
to spread the cost over an extended
period will help make

budgeting for
the visit a little easier for families.

We are very much looking forward to
what promises to be a

fantastic and
memorable experience for our Year 4
children!

Remembrance Day – Uniformed
Organisations

As part of our

Remembrance Day
commemorations

, we would like to
invite any children who are members
of a uniformed service organisation,
such as

Scouts, Guides, Cubs,
Brownies, Cadets, St John
Ambulance

, or a similar group, to
proudly wear their

service uniform to
school on Wednesday 11th November

Children who are not members of a
uniformed organisation should attend
school in their

usual school uniform

We look forward to coming together
as a school community to mark this
important occasion and to reflect
upon and remember the sacrifices
made by those who have served, and
those who continue to serve.

Children in Need 2026 – Dress Up
and Donate!

We’re excited to support Children in
Need again this year with a fun
challenge for all pupils! On

Friday
13th November

, children are invited
to come to school dressed in
something bright, cheerful, and
smile-inducing—from Pudsey-themed
outfits to superheroes or their own
creative designs. Alongside their
joyful attire, we kindly ask for a small
donation to help raise funds for this
amazing cause, supporting children
and young people across the UK.
Let’s celebrate creativity, kindness,
and community spirit!

Win a Giant Pudsey Bear! 🐻

As part of our fundraising, we are
delighted to offer children the
exciting opportunity to

win a Giant
Pudsey Bear!

Children can enter the prize draw by
making a £1 donation per entry. On

Friday 13th November

, one number
will be selected at random and the
lucky ticket holder will take home the
Giant Pudsey Bear.

Donations can be made

online or
directly through the School Office

. We
hope lots of our children will get
involved and help us raise as much as
possible for this fantastic cause.

Thank you for your continued
generosity and support, and good luck
to all our entrants!

🐻💛

Reminder: School Gates at Drop-
Off & Collection

A polite reminder to all parents and
carers that the

Visitor Gate at the
front of the school is for visitors and
latecomers

only.

For the safety of our children and to
help keep arrival and collection times
running smoothly,

all parents and
carers dropping off or collecting
children should use the designated
side gates.

We kindly ask that you

do not use the
Visitor Gate as an entrance or exit
during normal drop-off and collection
times.

Thank you for your understanding
and cooperation in helping us keep
our school site

safe, secure and well
organised.

Birthday Treats & Food in School

Following careful consideration, we
have decided that

sweets, chocolates,
cakes or other food treats should not
be brought into school to share with
classmates

, including for birthdays
and other celebrations. This is to help
us keep all children safe, particularly
those with serious or potentially life-
threatening allergies.

We also kindly remind families that

packed lunches should contain
healthy choices and must not include
sweets or chocolate

. As we operate a

nut-free approach

, please do not send
in foods containing nuts, including
peanut butter, Nutella, cereal bars
containing nuts or products labelled

“may contain nuts.”

We absolutely want children to feel
special on their birthdays! Families
are welcome to consider

non-food
alternatives

, such as stickers, small
stationery items or donating a
birthday book to the class or school
library.

Thank you for your understanding
and continued support in helping us
keep

every child safe and included.

YDP Wraparound Provision:
Booking Reminder

A reminder to parents and carers
wishing to book their child into the

wraparound provision provided by
YDP

that all bookings must be made
directly through the YDP booking
platform, which can be found

HERE

.
Please note that

YDP is a separate
provider

, and therefore the school
office is

unable to make or manage
bookings on behalf of families

Places are limited, so we strongly
encourage families to book as far in
advance as possible to avoid
disappointment.

If you need to make
a

same-day booking

, this must be
completed through the YDP booking
platform

by 1.00pm at the latest

. We
are also pleased to share that YDP
has informed us that they will be
taking on an

additional member of
staff on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and
Thursdays

, which will increase
capacity and allow

more spaces to
become available on these days

Thank you for your cooperation and
for ensuring all bookings are made
directly with YDP.

Uniform Donations

We are very grateful for all the
uniform donations we receive.
However,

we kindly ask that parents
and carers do not bring any more
uniform donations into school at this
time,

as we currently have plenty of
stock. The only items we are still able
to accept are

clean, good-condition
uniform with the school logo

,
specifically:

Jumpers and cardigans

PE tops

Hoodies

Thank you for your understanding
and continued support.

announcements.title: EEBSA-Environmental and Emotional Barriers to Scho
announcements.content:
EEBSA

-Environmental

and Emotional

Barriers to

School

Attendance

Environmental and Emotional
Barriers to School Attendance
(EEBSA) is a term used to describe a
child's difficulty attending or
engaging with school due to
emotional factors. Children may
display EEBSA in a variety of ways,
and recognising the early signs can
help ensure they receive the right
support (please see the image
provided by Cambridgeshire County
Council highlighting signs of
EEBSA).

If you have concerns that your child
may be showing signs of EEBSA,
please speak to your child's class
teacher or a member of the Senior
Leadership Team. By working
together, we can develop a shared
understanding of your child's
strengths and any barriers they may
be facing, with the aim of supporting
their wellbeing and helping them feel
happy and successful at school.

Miss Westwood

will be hosting an
informal

Coffee Afternoon on
Wednesday 18th November from
2:30pm to 3:00pm

. Parents and carers
are warmly invited to attend to find
out more about EEBSA, discuss any
concerns, and learn about the support
available.

We look forward to seeing you there.

announcements.title: Attendance Update: Termly Pizza Parties (TAPP) & Appointment Guidelines
announcements.content:
Attendance Update

Medical appointments

will continue
to be authorised only when
appointment confirmation is provided
to the school office.

Optician
appointments

will no longer be
authorised from September, as these
can usually be arranged outside
school hours.

We are also delighted to launch our

Termly Attendance Pizza Parties
(TAPP).

Pupils achieving

98%
attendance or above

each term will be
invited to a special pizza party during
the final week of term and will
receive a raffle ticket for the chance
to win a

£50 Amazon voucher.

At Warboys Primary Academy, we
know that good attendance plays a
vital role in children's academic
achievement, social development and
wellbeing. Thank you for your
continued support in helping your
child attend school regularly and
arrive on time, giving them the very
best opportunity to thrive.

Term-time leave

We appreciate that unexpected events
can happen, and we’re always here to
support families where possible.

However, Cambridgeshire County
Council and the Department for
Education require schools to
authorise leave

only in exceptional
circumstances

—meaning rare,
unavoidable events.

Routine family holidays or planned
trips unfortunately do not meet this
threshold. You can find further
information here:

Non-attendance at school and the
law | Cambridgeshire County
Council

Thank you for your understanding
and cooperation.

announcements.title: Young Carers: Support & Parent Concern Form
announcements.content:
At our school, we are proud to
support our Young Carers and
recognise the important role they
play within their families. We work
closely with Centre 33 to provide
external support, while internally we
offer fortnightly Young Carers
sessions where children can come
together to chat, share experiences,
take part in activities, and relax in a
supportive environment. Led by Miss
Coles and Mrs Flisher, with support
from Mr Bostock, these sessions help
ensure our Young Carers feel valued,
understood, and supported. We are
also committed to raising awareness
across the school community and
celebrating the dedication, resilience,
and compassion shown by our Young
Carers every day.

Please follow the link below to flag
any child that you may deem to be a
Young Carer. A Young Carer is a
child young person who helps to look
after a family member who may have
an illness, disability, mental health
difficulty, or who may need extra
support for another reason. This care
can include practical tasks, emotional
support, or helping siblings, and it
may take place before or after the
school day. We recognise that these
responsibilities can sometimes impact
a child’s wellbeing, learning, and
emotional needs. All conversations
and responses will be treated
sensitively and in confidence.

Young Carers Parent Concern form –
Fill in form

Welcome to this week’s school

A very warm welcome back to all of
our children and families after the
October half-term break. We hope you
all enjoyed a wonderful week with
family and friends and had the
opportunity to relax, recharge and
make some special memories
together.

It has been lovely to see the school
buzzing with energy once again, and
what a fantastic way to end the week!
Our EYFS and KS1 children
thoroughly enjoyed taking part in a
vibrant

,

newsletter!

A very warm welcome back to all of
our children and families after the
October half-term break. We hope you

together.

vibrant

celebration.

meaningful and exciting week ahead

Remembrance Day

Children in Need 2026

. Please see
below for further information about
both of these events and how our
school community will be taking part.

recently arrived today and have been
sent home with children.

Thank you, as always, for your
continued support. We wish you all a
happy, safe and relaxing weekend,
and we look forward to seeing
everyone back in school on Monday.

Have a wonderful weekend!

Poundland issues major update as UK stores at risk of closure
metadata.contentSnippet: Poundland has issued an update today (November 12) as it continues to try to secure a potential rescue deal.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Poundland issues major update as UK stores at risk of closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Poundland has issued an update today (November 12), following the end of a 10-day period that allowed it to continue to try and secure a potential rescue deal. In recent months, the future of Poundland has been uncertain, with last-ditch efforts hoping to save the struggling retailer. The chain filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of October, which expired at midnight last night. Asked if the company was going into administration on Thursday, managing director Barry Williams told reporters: “We’re going to go and have a board meeting now to have those conversations.” Now, Poundland has issued an update, informing customers of its future plans. Poundland customers have been assured that its stores are open as normal for at least the next 10 working days. The Board of Poundland Limited said: “Over the past two weeks, Poundland has been operating under the statutory protection of a Notice of Intention (NOI) to appoint Administrators. “Amid an ongoing sale process, and with funding agreed to enable the business to continue trading during this period, the Board of Poundland has today resolved to make an application for a second NOI with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people. “This extends the current protections over the business for a further 10 working days. “Our stores remain open as usual during this period, and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.” Poundland has roughly 600 shops and 11,000 employees across the UK. Ahead of the announcement, Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice said: “Hopefully the directors will be able to extend the notice of administration period from tonight to allow time for a deal to be done with a new buyer for Poundland. “This will protect many thousands of jobs and keep an important value retailer on the High Street, for hard-pressed consumers worried about rising bills.” After a meeting with MPs on the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, Mr Williams thanked the chain’s staff, whose jobs are at risk. He told Sky News he was “representing 11,000 colleagues” as well as thousands in the broader supply chain and “maybe even the retail industry” at the meeting. Asked whether he could guarantee the security of jobs and keep the business going in the run-up to Christmas, he said there were “no guarantees at this point”. It is understood that Poundland’s owners, Gordon Brothers, have enabled the release of around £10 million of funding for things such as paying staff, taxes and suppliers of stock. The extension to Wednesday’s deadline could mean the prospect of a deal that would satisfy the company’s creditors remains on the table. Advisers have been in talks with parties interested in buying the brand or parts of the business such as swathes of shops. Recommended reading: It has held talks with potential bidders including Tesco over proposals to buy up to 150 stores, and other chains such as Iceland and Lidl. Investment firm Xyra Holdings emerged as a potential buyer for the whole business, while Irish firm Martin Property Group is believed to remain interested. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a takeover offer from Martin Property Group but management named the firm as the preferred bidder last month. Would you like to see Poundland remain on UK high streets? Let us know in the comments below.

metadata.contentSnippet: Every household in the UK is legally required to have a TV licence in order to watch or record live TV, regardless of what channel it is on

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: BBC TV Licence fee reduced from £180 to £7.50 for some in UK - are you eligible?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The TV licence fee is being reduced to £7.50 for some people in the UK, but you will need to check if you are eligible. Every household in the UK is legally required to have a TV licence in order to watch or record live TV, regardless of what channel it is on. Currently the cost of a colour TV licence is £180, however, some people in the UK could get that reduced to £7.50. Guidance from Gov.UK explains: “You can get a TV Licence for £7.50 if you live in an eligible residential care home, supported housing or sheltered accommodation. “You must be either retired and over 60 or disabled. Your housing manager can check if you can get it and will apply for you.” You can see the full guidance here. For those of us aged 75 or over who are in receipt of Pension Credit, the TV Licence can be obtained for free. Guidance from TV Licensing says: “Free TV Licences are only available if you’re 75 or over and you, or your partner living at the same address, are receiving Pension Credit. “If you think you’re eligible for a free licence but can’t apply online, please call 0300 790 6117* and speak to one of our advisors to request an application form (our lines are open between 8.30am and 6.30pm, from Monday to Friday). “Once we’ve received your application it may take a few weeks to process. If there are any problems we’ll write to let you know. We may also call you if you have given us your phone number. “There are separate arrangements in place for over 75s on the Isle of Man, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey.” You do not need a TV Licence to watch: You do need a TV Licence if you:

metadata.title: HMRC Child Benefit rates to rise in April 2027 - new payment amounts explained
metadata.contentSnippet: HMRC has updated its Child Benefit rates for 2027/28, with millions of parents set to receive higher weekly payments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: HMRC Child Benefit rates to rise in April 2027 - new payment amounts explained
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: HMRC has revealed that millions of families could receive more money in Child Benefit from next April, with new weekly payment rates now appearing on the Government's website. Parents currently receive £27.05 a week for their eldest or only child, with an additional £17.90 paid for each other child. However, these payments are set to increase again for the 2027/28 tax year, according to an update to the Government's Child Benefit information page on November 10. The provisional figures show that the weekly rate for an eldest or only child will rise to £28, while payments for each additional child are expected to increase to £18.55. This would give families an extra £49.40 a year for their eldest or only child, and an additional £33.80 annually for every other child they claim for. The figures are currently marked as 'provisional', meaning they are not yet confirmed as final rates. However, the Government website's update history shows that previous provisional Child Benefit rates have subsequently matched the final amounts announced. The weekly rate of Guardian's Allowance is also expected to increase, rising from £22.95 in 2026/27 to £23.75 in 2027/28. Guardian's Allowance is an additional payment for people bringing up a child whose parents have died. In some circumstances, it can also be claimed where one parent has died and the surviving parent cannot look after the child. Child Benefit is available to parents or guardians responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if they remain in approved education or training. Only one person can claim Child Benefit for each child, but there is now no limit on the number of children families can receive payments for. This follows the abolition of the two-child limit in April this year. Previously, the restriction meant parents could generally only claim Child Benefit for a maximum of two children. However, some families may face a tax charge if their earnings exceed the High Income Child Benefit Charge threshold. The charge applies if either parent has an individual income of more than £60,000 in tax years from 2024/25 onwards. For tax years up to and including 2023/24, the threshold was £50,000. Child Benefit is usually paid directly into a claimant's bank account every four weeks. Claiming also provides valuable National Insurance credits, which can help protect a parent's entitlement to the State Pension.

metadata.title: More than one million yellow box fines issued - what are the rules and how to appeal
metadata.contentSnippet: More than a million yellow box junction penalties issued by councils in England and Wales since 2023, the junction rules and how to challenge a notice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than one million yellow box fines issued - what are the rules and how to appeal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than a million yellow box junction penalties have been issued by councils in England and Wales since 2023, research suggests. Used car retailer cinch said 37 councils reported issuing 1,047,472 penalty charge notices between 2023 and 2026, with nearly £58 million in penalty payments also reported. The company sent Freedom of Information requests to 217 authorities across the UK, but the penalty figures reported are not a total for every council or for the whole country. The underlying council responses were not supplied with the release and could not be independently checked. Its figures include 347,614 notices in 2025 and a further 231,458 in 2026 up to July. In Hackney, the number rose from 314 in 2024 to 8,567 in 2025, while Buckinghamshire recorded an increase from 3,618 to 16,120. Liverpool recorded 7,622 notices in 2025, compared with 3,376 the year before, according to the research. At Dennis Road Roundabout in Surrey, the number rose from 1,557 in 2024 to 9,101 in 2025. Cinch said councils had received more than 100,000 challenges since 2023 and accepted over 18,000. Those included 6,954 accepted challenges in Redbridge out of 27,615 received, and 3,582 out of 8,328 in Cardiff. Ben Welham, a motoring expert at cinch, said: "Yellow box junctions help to keep traffic moving, but they can be difficult to navigate, particularly in busy towns and cities where traffic is constantly stopping and starting." Yellow box junctions have criss-cross markings designed to keep traffic from blocking the road. Under rule 174 of the Highway Code, drivers must not enter until their exit road or lane is clear. There is an exception for drivers turning right who are held up only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right. At a signalled roundabout, drivers must not enter a box unless they can cross it completely without stopping. The Northern Ireland Highway Code sets out the same box-junction rules. Penalty amounts and payment periods depend on the issuing authority, so motorists should check the details on their notice. For example, Newcastle City Council says its yellow box penalty is £70, reduced to £35 if paid within 21 days. In England and Wales, a motorist who believes a council PCN is wrong can make a formal challenge, known as a representation, to the authority that issued it. Cinch says drivers generally have 28 days to challenge a notice and should provide supporting evidence, such as photographs or available camera footage. Check the notice for the applicable deadline and instructions, including how to view any footage. If the authority rejects the formal challenge, GOV.UK says there are 28 days after receiving the rejection notice to appeal to an independent tribunal. The appeal is made to London Tribunals for a PCN issued in London, or the Traffic Penalty Tribunal for one issued elsewhere in England or Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different appeal arrangements, so drivers there should follow the instructions from the issuing body. If an appeal is successful, the PCN is cancelled and the motorist does not have to pay.

metadata.title: Police share fresh update after boy falls from double-decker bus
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have shared a fresh update on a 14-year-old boy who fell out of a double-decker bus in Wimblington.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police share fresh update after boy falls from double-decker bus
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have shared a fresh update on a 14-year-old boy who fell from a double-decker bus in Cambridgeshire. Emergency services were called to the incident which shut Doddington Road, Wimblington, at around 3.45pm on October 14. The boy was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, with serious but not life threatening injuries, it was confirmed. The East of England Ambulance Service sent an ambulance, an ambulance officer vehicle and the Magpas Air Ambulance. It was later revealed the bus had been carrying students from Cromwell Community College, in Chatteris, at the time of the incident. In a fresh update on Thursday (November 12), Cambridgeshire Police revealed the victim is now out of hospital and at home. Cambridgeshire County Council confirmed the bus involved was a council-commissioned Home to School Transport Service. A spokesperson revealed the local authority's health and safety team is now investigating the incident. They said: "We are working closely with the police and the operator and will be fully investigating the circumstances around this serious incident. "Our thoughts are with the family and the child affected. We wish them a full and swift recovery." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections
metadata.contentSnippet: A decision looms on a plan for up to 600 new homes on land near Priory Hill Road in St Neots, despite a flood of objections from residents.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A decision looms on a plan for up to 600 new homes in St Neots, despite a flood of objections from residents. The outline application by Bloor Homes for land at Priory Hill, north of St Neots, is set to be considered by Huntingdonshire District Council's (HDC) development management committee on November 16. The 87-hectare site would create a new neighbourhood between Priory Hill Road, Huntingdon Road, the River Great Ouse, and the East Coast Main Line. An illustrative sketch of the land in St Neots where 600 new homes could be built (Image: Bloor Homes) The scheme seeks permission for up to 600 homes, with 40 per cent designated as affordable housing. Alongside the housing, the plans include a community hub, mobility hub, public open space, allotments, walking and cycling routes, landscaping, and associated infrastructure. Around 64 hectares of the site would be retained as green space, including meadows, parkland, wildlife areas, and sustainable drainage features. Developers say the plans would extend Priory Park northwards, creating a new 'Priory Piece', new pedestrian and cycle links, and providing opportunities for a future footbridge across the River Great Ouse connecting to Paxton Pits Nature Reserve and the Ouse Valley Way. The site sits close to Priory Park (Image: Newsquest) For access to the site, the plans would see two new T-junctions introduced on Priory Hill Road. Road speeds would be reduced to 30mph along Priory Hill Road and Huntingdon Road, with additional traffic-calming measures. In addition, the double-mini roundabout at the B1043 Huntingdon Road, Priory Hill Road and Mill Lane intersection would be changed to a staggered T-junction, as the developers claim it had previously been identified as "a safety concern". The double-mini roundabout at Priory Hill Road (Image: Newsquest) The double-mini roundabout near the site could be changed to a staggered T-junction (Image: Newsquest) Members of the development management committee are expected to make a decision on the application at a meeting at 7pm on November 16. Planning officers are recommending that the scheme be approved subject to conditions, or refused if an S106 agreement has not been reached. St Neots Town Council and Little Paxton Parish Council have both lodged objections to the scheme. The town council said it is concerned that "the development would place additional pressure on local services and infrastructure, particularly secondary school provision" and raised additional concerns over loss of agricultural land, flood risk and drainage. Additionally, HDC has received a total of 92 objections from residents. One neighbour wrote: "It would cause demonstrable harm to infrastructure, landscape, biodiversity, and the wellbeing of existing residents. "I therefore respectfully urge Huntingdonshire District Council to refuse planning permission for this development." What do you think about the plans? Leave a comment on this story or contact emily.stevens@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits
metadata.contentSnippet: Practice Radar figures show 53 per cent of children in Huntingdon saw an NHS dentist in the year to March 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Just under half of young children in Huntingdon are missing out on NHS dental care, which is below the national average. Practice Radar figures show 53 per cent of children in Huntingdon saw an NHS dentist in the year to March 2026. That compares with 58 per cent across England when measured on the same basis. The gap is even wider among younger children, with just 41.3 per cent of those aged between one and five in Huntingdon seeing an NHS dentist during the year. The figures come amid ongoing national concerns about access to NHS dentistry, especially for younger children. Practice Radar analysed NHS Business Services Authority data to estimate child dental attendance in all 543 English constituencies. The analysis found large regional differences, with the proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist ranging from 32.2 per cent in the City of London and Westminster to 74.5 per cent in Sheffield Hallam. In 62 constituencies, fewer than half of children saw an NHS dentist during the year. Huntingdon’s 53 per cent rate is five points below the England average, but the area is not among the worst performers. The study also examined tooth decay among five-year-olds, but those figures are reported by council area rather than constituency. In Huntingdonshire, 11.4 per cent of five-year-olds had experienced tooth decay in the 2023/24 survey, compared with 22.4 per cent nationally. Huntingdon is therefore not among the 60 constituencies with below-average NHS dental attendance and significantly higher childhood tooth decay. Practice Radar warned that the two figures cover different geographic areas. The 53 per cent attendance rate covers children living in Huntingdon, while the 11.4 per cent decay rate covers the wider Huntingdonshire council area. The research also examined NHS dental contracts in the area. The analysis included seven NHS general dental contracts in Huntingdon, with a median payment of £34.51 per unit of dental activity (UDA). A UDA is the NHS measure for dental work, with different treatments given different values. Across England, the median constituency had an NHS dentist visit rate of 58.6 per cent for children and 47.5 per cent for one- to five-year-olds. Fewer than 40 per cent of one- to five-year-olds saw an NHS dentist in 111 constituencies. There are signs of improvement across England, with 508 out of 543 constituencies recording a higher proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist compared to two years earlier. However, the researchers emphasised that the figures only cover NHS dental care. Children treated entirely privately are excluded, so the figures do not show how many receive dental care overall. Children are counted by where they live, not where their dentist is based, so some Huntingdon residents may receive care outside the constituency. The analysis used NHS Dental Statistics for England 2025/26, tooth-decay data from the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities and population estimates from the Office for National Statistics. A recent Cambridgeshire MP survey found nearly half of respondents were not registered with an NHS dentist, while about half had paid privately after struggling to access NHS treatment. Local NHS dentists have told an MP that contracts are financially and operationally "unviable", with practices losing money on NHS work and subsidising it through private income.

metadata.title: Investigation after boy assaulted at Cambridgeshire school remains ongoing
metadata.contentSnippet: An investigation launched after a student was allegedly assaulted at Cromwell Community College in Chatteris is ongoing after more than seven weeks.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Investigation after boy assaulted at Cambridgeshire school remains ongoing
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An investigation launched after a student was allegedly assaulted at a Cambridgeshire school is ongoing after more than seven weeks. Police received a report of an assault at Cromwell Community College, in Chatteris, on Wednesday (September 23). The incident was said to have taken place earlier in the day, Cambridgeshire Constabulary confirmed. The victim, a 13-year-old boy, attended hospital for treatment to his injuries and a crime for grievous bodily harm was raised. In a statement, the Active Learning Trust, which runs the school, revealed a Year 9 student was "hurt in an incident" . A spokesperson said staff "responded quickly and appropriately" and gave "care and support to the injured student". They added: "The college’s pastoral team has been supporting students following the incident and will continue to offer reassurance as required. "We will co-operate fully with the police and their investigation into this matter." In an update on Thursday (November 12), Cambridgeshire Police confirmed the investigation remains ongoing. metadata.title: Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure
metadata.contentSnippet: Families of adults with learning disabilities have raised concerns over plans to move a Cambridgeshire County Council day service from St Ives to Huntingdon with just five weeks' notice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families of adults with learning disabilities have raised concerns over plans to move a Huntingdonshire day service from St Ives to Huntingdon with just five weeks' notice. Cambridgeshire County Council has told users of the CATS centre in Bull Lane, St Ives, their families, carers and advocates that the service is due to move to Huntingdon Community Centre on December 7. In a November 2 letter, Cambridgeshire head of provider services Mandy Langley told the Singh family that activities and support would move to the Huntingdon centre, around six miles away. The family says the letter was the first it knew about the plans and questions why relatives were not consulted before the announcement. Surj Singh said his brother has Down syndrome, is non-verbal and relies heavily on familiar people and surroundings. He said the family feared moving the service could seriously affect his brother and others who rely on familiar routines. The family has questioned whether the new centre is suitable, citing noise, summer heat, staffing, supervision, privacy, facilities and personal care. The Singh family complained to the council on November 5 and asked it to pause the move until families had been consulted and individual needs and transition plans addressed. Mr Singh said his brother’s needs raised serious questions about whether the new setting and arrangements would suit him and others with different support needs. The family wants to know when the decision was made, what assessment and consultation took place, and how staffing, personal care and individual suitability will be assured. Mr Singh said his brother had been away from the service because of ill health, and the family had spent weeks planning his return with social services and the provider without hearing about the move. The family has also questioned the move’s timing, just weeks before Christmas. The council said the move was planned because fewer people were using CATS St Ives. It said Huntingdon Community Centre already provides day services and has room for St Ives users, allowing it to "make better use of our buildings and resources". The council said familiar staff would continue supporting users and similar activities would be available in Huntingdon. But Mr Singh said the family feared the Huntingdon centre was much larger and noisier than the St Ives site. The council said users would still have access to the St Ives community while being offered opportunities in Huntingdon. The council said users would be offered extra visits to the Huntingdon centre in November to prepare for the move. It said there would be no break in service and that the St Ives centre would operate until the move. The council said it would discuss any changes to care arrangements or transport with those affected. The letter said: "We are committed to supporting everyone through this change and making it as smooth as possible." The family says the council has acknowledged its complaint but has yet to answer its concerns. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: "From Monday, December 7, the council will be bringing together the CATS day service in St Ives with services provided at Huntingdon Community Centre for adults with learning disabilities. "Huntingdon Community Centre already provides a wide range of activities and opportunities, including the Blossom and Bloom Café and TAG Bikes. "Bringing the services together will give people attending CATS access to a broader choice of activities, opportunities to build confidence and independence, and the chance to meet and develop relationships with new people. "Our priority is to ensure a smooth transition for everyone affected, and we will continue to work with individuals and their families throughout the process, including reviewing any transport arrangements required. "The move will also bring services together on one site, providing greater operational resilience and making the best use of council resources. “We can confirm this complaint is being investigated and we have contacted the family to explain the complaints process."

metadata.title: Doctor Who stars Peter Davison and Paul McGann to visit Peterborough exhibition
metadata.contentSnippet: Doctor Who stars are set to bring a touch of time travel to Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Doctor Who stars Peter Davison and Paul McGann to visit Peterborough exhibition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Doctor Who stars are set to bring a touch of time travel to Peterborough. Peter Davison and Paul McGann, who played the Fifth and Eighth Doctors, will visit Queensgate Shopping Centre on Saturday, November 21, from 12pm to 3pm as part of the centre’s Christmas lights switch-on. Their appearance comes just days before the opening of the Whoseum, an unofficial Doctor Who exhibition celebrating 63 years of the iconic sci-fi series. Derek Handley, exhibition curator, said: "After last year, people kept asking me how we could top what we had achieved at the museum. I think we've found a way to do it." The Whoseum will officially open on Monday, November 23, and will feature monsters, costumes, original props and recreated sets from the long-running series. Located in Unit 79 at Queensgate, the exhibition is created by Rapido Trains in association with Peterborough Museum and Art Gallery. It promises to take visitors on a journey through time and space, exploring the creativity behind some of Doctor Who’s most memorable creatures. Jason Shron, president of Rapido Trains, said: "For over 50 years, Doctor Who exhibitions have been a way for the fan community to engage with the original props and costumes of their favourite television programme. "I'm delighted that Rapido Trains has helped bring the Whoseum to life, including some of my own costumes made by the talented Rob Allsopp, who was a bona fide monster maker for Doctor Who. "I hope that Whovians all over the UK and around the world will make the trip to Peterborough to take a walk through Doctor Who history." The exhibition will reveal how these monsters were designed and built, offering insight into their cultural impact. Sarah Wilson, heritage manager at Peterborough Museum, said: "I'm delighted that the monsters are coming back in force, thanks to our team from last year and Rapido Trains, and in such a spectacular way, with the inside of the TARDIS and a Dalek spaceship being brought back to life from long-lost Doctor Who episodes from 60 years ago. "Only this time, you can see them for real." From January 2027, the Whoseum will double in size, expanding to fill the entire unit and showcase even more monsters, props and sets. A spokesperson said it will offer fans another chance to experience something new in the new year, with further supporting exhibitions planned throughout 2027.

metadata.title: Herts and Cambs residents urged to get winter-ready with three simple steps
metadata.contentSnippet: The NHS is urging people in Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire to take simple steps now to protect their health and prepare for winter.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Herts and Cambs residents urged to get winter-ready with three simple steps
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People in Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire are urged to take simple steps now to protect their health and prepare for winter. The advice comes from NHS Central East’s Get Winter Ready campaign, which helps people “protect, prepare and stay well” through the colder months. The campaign covers Bedfordshire, Luton, Milton Keynes, Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Hertfordshire. Dr Fiona Head, medical director at NHS Central East Integrated Care Board, said: "There are simple things we can all do to help ourselves and those around us stay well this winter. "One of the most important is getting vaccinated if you’re eligible, to help protect yourself and those around you. "Flu and COVID-19 can cause serious illness, particularly for those who are more vulnerable, and vaccination can help reduce your risk of becoming seriously unwell. "It's also important to be prepared. Make sure you have the medicines you need at home and order repeat prescriptions in good time. "If you do become unwell, knowing where to go can help you get the right advice and support, whether that’s from your local pharmacy or NHS 111." The campaign urges people to protect themselves, prepare for winter and stay well. 'Protect' focuses on getting eligible flu and COVID-19 vaccinations, practising good hygiene, and taking care around others when unwell to help prevent the spread of illness. 'Prepare' is about keeping everyday medicines at home, ordering repeat prescriptions early, and using the NHS App to order repeat prescriptions. 'Stay well' encourages people to look after both their physical and mental health, and to use the right services when they need support, such as Pharmacy First for many common conditions or NHS 111 when they need urgent medical help but are unsure what to do. Dr Head said: "Winter is a challenging time for health services, and we’re working closely with our NHS providers and partners across the region to prepare for the months ahead. "We want people to stay safe and well, but we also want everyone to know that the NHS is here when they need it." More information and practical advice are available on the Get Winter Ready: Protect, Prepare, Stay Well webpage.

metadata.title: Air ambulance teams safely trial hospital treatment for prolonged cardiac arrests
metadata.contentSnippet: East Anglian Air Ambulance has successfully trialled a hospital treatment for patients in prolonged cardiac arrest at emergency scenes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Air ambulance teams safely trial hospital treatment for prolonged cardiac arrests
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: East Anglian Air Ambulance has successfully trialled a hospital treatment for patients in prolonged cardiac arrest at emergency scenes. EAAA teams used the treatment on patients in prolonged cardiac arrest outside hospital as part of the ERICA-ARREST feasibility study. The study tested whether helicopter emergency medical service clinicians could safely use resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) to improve blood flow to the heart and brain during resuscitation. Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) is a minimally invasive procedure that involves inserting and inflating a balloon within the aorta to temporarily control blood flow. (Image: East Anglian Air Ambulance) Dr James Price, consultant emergency physician at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and HEMS consultant and consultant lead for research and development at EAAA, said: "Patients who remain in cardiac arrest despite prolonged resuscitation efforts currently have very limited treatment options and face extremely poor outcomes. "Our study has shown that REBOA can be delivered safely by pre-hospital critical care teams and can improve blood pressure during cardiac arrest, helping to direct blood flow to the organs that matter most. "While this study was not designed to determine whether REBOA improves survival, these findings provide a strong foundation for further research and represent an important step forward in exploring new treatment options for this group of patients." Hospitals typically use REBOA to control severe internal bleeding. Doctors insert a small balloon through a groin artery and inflate it inside the aorta, the body’s main artery. Inflating the balloon temporarily blocks blood flow to the lower body and redirects it to the heart and brain. The study tested whether the technique could help patients whose hearts would not restart after prolonged, high-quality resuscitation. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains a major cause of death, and survival rates for patients experiencing prolonged cardiac arrest have not improved in 50 years. The study included 39 patients, aged 58.7 on average, who suffered non-traumatic cardiac arrests outside hospital and did not respond to advanced resuscitation. Doctors attempted REBOA a median of 51 minutes after cardiac arrest, at a very advanced stage of resuscitation. Researchers found HEMS clinicians could perform the procedure safely, with no related complications reported. After inflation, diastolic blood pressure rose by an average of 59 per cent, directing more pressure towards the heart and brain. Of the 33 patients in whom aortic blockage was confirmed, 24.2 per cent achieved a sustained return of spontaneous circulation, and 6.1 per cent survived to hospital discharge. However, researchers emphasised that the study was not intended to determine whether REBOA improves survival, as it did not include a control group. It instead tested whether the procedure was safe outside hospital and improved circulation as expected. Dr Price said the study followed years of work building the clinical skills, safeguards and research systems needed for such a complex treatment before hospital. The research was carried out by EAAA’s research, audit, innovation, and development (RAID) group. He said: "East Anglian Air Ambulance is first and foremost a regional charity looking after critically ill and injured patients across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, but alongside that clinical work we have built a research programme led by clinicians who look after these patients every day and want to find better ways of treating them, and ultimately save more lives." He added that the programme had improved EAAA’s overall care, beyond the ERICA-ARREST study. EAAA regularly responds to cardiac arrests across its region, which account for up to 30 per cent of the charity’s medical call-outs. Its teams deliver advanced critical care normally available only in hospital. Researchers say the findings justify further study of whether the treatment improves survival.

metadata.title: New illegal Fire Stick warning issued as police investigating financial records
metadata.contentSnippet: Those using illegal Fire Sticks have been warned that police are now using financial records to find those culpable.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New illegal Fire Stick warning issued as police investigating financial records
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fresh illegal Fire Stick warning has been issued after police are cracking down on users by tracing payments through sellers’ bank accounts. The alert comes amid growing concerns over the widespread use of modified TV Fire Sticks and so-called “dodgy boxes”. These devices enable users to access premium content from providers such as Sky, TNT Sports, Disney+, and Netflix for free. However, those using the devices have been warned that police are now using financial records to find those culpable. Former detective Rav Wilding issued the warning during an appearance on BBC Morning Live. He explained that police are investigating financial records linked to the sale of modified Fire Sticks, which allow users to access premium TV content for free. Mr Wilding said: "They’re going for the distributors. "They’re going for the sellers. "They are having a lot of success. "But actually, once they’ve got the seller, they’re going through their accounts. "They’re seeing who has been paying the money for these illegal things, and if they’ve been paying them for these sticks then people should possibly expect a conversation or two if the police want to know why they’ve been paying them money for this." The illegal devices typically cost between £30 and £100 and provide unauthorised access to subscription-only TV services, including live football. Although owning a standard Fire Stick is legal, Mr Wilding said using one to stream pirated content is a crime. He said: "It’s a crime. "It’s not allowed. "Owning the stick itself is not a crime, but using it for this purpose is. "They (subscription service providers) are losing money to this, so they have been reaching out and are taking action against those people using them illegally as well. "So I wouldn’t say it’s something you should do. "It is actually a crime and it can have a nasty fine, a huge fine and also a custodial sentence for users and sellers of these things." In the UK, downloading or streaming pirated content can be a crime, but prosecutions of individual viewers remain extremely rare. Despite this, several people have been jailed this year as the clampdown on illegal streaming devices in the UK continues. Recommended reading: Those caught using or selling a 'dodgy' fire stick/box and streaming premium content without paying are in breach of Section 11 of the Fraud Act 2006. It says a person will be in breach if they obtain services "without any payment having been made for or in respect of them or without payment having been made in full". A person found guilty of this kind of offence could face a hefty fine, or even a prison sentence in extreme cases. What is your favourite TV show to watch? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans are set to be approved to replace “potentially unsafe cladding” on blocks of flats in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans are set to be approved to replace “potentially unsafe cladding” on blocks of flats in Cambridgeshire. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority’s growth committee recommended the new Local Remediation Acceleration Plan, or LRAP, be approved. The plan details the authority’s strategy for replacing cladding which does not meet fire safety standards on residential buildings of five stories or more. The building owner has ultimate responsibility for carrying out the work but a new bill currently being considered by Parliament could introduce fines of up to £500k for those who fail to fix the issues without delay. Cllr Sarah Conboy, chair of the committee, said: “This comes from a very difficult place, many of us will remember the heart-wrenching experience that happened at Grenfell. “The horrendous loss of life, but also the impact it had on a whole community as well as everybody involved in responding to that incident.” It was earlier revealed that there are ten high-rise flat buildings of seven stories or more in Cambridgeshire – all in Cambridge – which still need cladding replaced. “This was along with 62 medium-rise flats, of five or six stories, across the county according to the latest report presented to the committee. “It added that a few buildings have come in and out of scope 'during detailed assessment'. The combined authority has previously said they are “confident” in meeting the government’s targets that cladding on high-rises be replaced by the end of 2029 and end of 2031 for medium-rises – deadlines introduced in 2025. The updated plan, replacing the LRAP approved in 2025, addresses “key risks” including “landlord reluctance, contractor capacity and developer disputes”. The report presented to the committee added that “contractor capacity and quality of workmanship is a particular risk given this is a nationwide task”. Sean Hedger, the remediation manager, said that replacing cladding is a “lengthy process” which can take up to two years. He said he was concerned about the term “unsafe buildings” as it could worry residents, reassuring them that they are still safe to live in. He said: “Just because a building requires remediation of the external wall system it does not mean that the building is unsafe to live in. Responsible persons would often put in interim measures such as an upgraded fire alarm system to enable simultaneous evacuation instead of a stay put policy.” He said that in areas of the country where residents have had to move from their flats, this is “generally” due to “a mixture of fire safety and structural issues as well”. Cllr Ros Hathorn said this was “such important work” and they are the growth committee so their remit includes housing and development. She said: “Actually this is one of the most important things we need to do because Grenfell caused massive damage, but also damaged people’s confidence in living in flats. “And actually we need to rebuild that reassurance and until we do that it is going to be very challenging to respond to the housing crisis so this is such an important piece of work.” The committee recommended the plan be approved when it goes to the CPCA board for a final decision later this month.

metadata.title: St Ivo Academy students honour fallen at St Ives Remembrance parade
metadata.contentSnippet: Students from St Ivo Academy in St Ives gathered to remember the fallen for Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ivo Academy students honour fallen at St Ives Remembrance parade
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Students from St Ives gathered to remember the fallen for Remembrance Sunday and Armistice Day. St Ivo Academy students joined St Ives’ Remembrance Parade at the weekend and held a two-minute silence at school on Wednesday, November 11. The Salvation Army Band at St Ivo (Image: Astrea Academy Trust) Jessica Pearce, principal at St Ivo Academy, said: "Our students understand the importance of Remembrance Day and their participation in these ceremonies is a reflection of our school's commitment to honouring the past and also to thinking about the individuals and their families whose lives are affected by conflict around the world today. "It was incredibly moving to see our young people show such respect and dignity as they remembered those who gave so much for our freedom. Students at the St Ives Remembrance event (Image: Astrea Academy Trust) "Remembrance Day is not just about looking back; it's about understanding the impact of the past on our present and future. "Our students engaged deeply with this message, and we are proud of the way they represented our school within the community." The Salvation Army Band with headteacher Jessica Pearce (Image: Astrea Academy Trust) At the Remembrance Parade, students walked alongside residents, veterans and community leaders to pay their respects, and laid a wreath on behalf of the school. On Armistice Day, Royal British Legion chairman Alan Scott joined St Ivo students and staff for the silence. St Ivo students attending school in uniform for Armistice Day (Image: Astrea Academy Trust) The ceremony featured readings and a performance by the Salvation Army Band. St Ivo is committed to honour Remembrance Day each year to ensure the legacy of those who served is never forgotten.

metadata.title: Funding threat could render world-leading Cambridgeshire telescope defunct
metadata.contentSnippet: A world-leading telescope at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Cambridgeshire could be shut down if its funding is withdrawn.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Funding threat could render world-leading Cambridgeshire telescope defunct
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A world-leading radio telescope could be shut down if its funding is withdrawn. The Cambridge Telescope, at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Cambridgeshire, is one of seven e-MERLIN radio telescopes that work as a single powerful instrument. Its future is uncertain after the Science and Technology Facilities Council and UK Research and Innovation proposed ending all operational funding for e-MERLIN after March 2028. Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of South Cambridgeshire District Council, has written to the Secretary of State urging a review of the decision and warning of its potential impact on UK science. In a November 10 letter, she said ending funding without a replacement plan posed an "existential threat" to e-MERLIN and could leave the Cambridge Telescope "defunct." Cllr Smith said: "This is a world-leading scientific facility, right here on our doorstep, and we are facing the very real prospect of losing it. "Once we lose facilities like this, we can't simply bring them back. "Decades of expertise and scientific achievement could be lost for good. "It's extraordinary that the Government is talking about making Cambridge the engine of Britain's economic growth while allowing the funding to disappear from the very scientific infrastructure that makes this area so special. "The Government needs to put its money where its mouth is. "If Ministers are serious about backing Cambridge and British science, they need to step in and save this telescope." The telescope, owned and operated by the University of Manchester, works alongside six others across England. The network’s 200km spread gives it a 200km baseline and resolution comparable to the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. It has helped produce more than 1,000 peer-reviewed papers and supports thousands of researchers worldwide. The funding row comes as the Government promotes Greater Cambridge and the Oxford-Cambridge Growth Corridor as engines of economic growth. In her letter, Cllr Smith argued that e-MERLIN supports the wider research and innovation economy by attracting investment and creating highly skilled jobs in science and engineering. She warned that losing the facility could undermine the future success of the growth corridor. South Cambridgeshire MP Pippa Heylings also voiced concerns. Ms Heylings said: "Cambridge is known across the world for its ground-breaking science, and this telescope is part of what makes that possible. "You cannot build a world-leading science economy by dismantling the world-leading science facilities we already have. "Yet that is exactly what these cuts risk doing. "This isn't just about one telescope. "It's about the future of British science, the skilled jobs and expertise we depend on, and whether the Government is genuinely committed to the growth it keeps promising. "We need a proper long-term funding solution, not a decision that could throw away decades of scientific achievement." Cllr Smith has called on the Government to work with UKRI and STFC to find a sustainable long-term funding solution before the existing arrangements expire in March 2028. She also wants any final decision delayed until its scientific, economic and strategic effects are fully assessed. The letter was also sent to Liberal Democrat MPs Pippa Heylings, Ian Sollom and Charlotte Cane, and to the party’s science, innovation and technology spokesperson Victoria Collins. The observatory has also been the subject of concerns over East West Rail, with the University of Cambridge warning that electromagnetic interference and vibration could jeopardise research.
