metadata.title: How Virgin Media 02 customers can keep free emails as service ends
metadata.contentSnippet: Virgin Media email users face a choice over transferring to Junara. Find out which addresses are affected, the deadlines and the fees.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: How Virgin Media 02 customers can keep free emails as service ends
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Virgin Media is closing its free email service, leaving account holders to decide whether to transfer or move elsewhere. Users who want to keep their existing address can switch to Junara, an email provider owned by Atmail. The change affects addresses ending in virginmedia.com, virgin.net, ntlworld.com and blueyonder.co.uk. Virgin Media says it is contacting affected account holders in phases and they will have at least 45 days from the first communication to decide what to do. They can sign up with Junara, download their emails and data before moving to another provider, or close their account. Junara says users whose accounts are suspended after their deadline have another 120 days to sign up and reactivate them. After that period, the account and its data will be permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, the provider says. Virgin Media stopped offering email accounts to new customers in May 2022. Current Virgin Media broadband, landline or TV customers who move to Junara will be offered their first 12 months free, subject to a 99p transfer fee. Customers who have told Virgin Media they need additional support will be offered their first 18 months free. Former Virgin Media customers who no longer have those services will need to sign up to a standard Junara plan to keep their email service. Those who do not want to transfer can download their data and move to another provider, including a free service. Virgin Media says its messages about the change will not include clickable sign-up links, and customers should be cautious of unexpected requests for personal details, passwords or payment information. A Virgin Media spokesperson said: "As we focus and prioritise our investments and resource on ensuring our customers have the best connectivity experience, we've taken the decision to close the remaining Virgin Media email accounts. "We are transferring our email service to Junara, a specialist cloud-based email provider owned by Atmail, giving users a clear route to keep their existing Virgin Media email address if they choose to. "We're writing directly to all impacted customers to clearly explain the changes and will provide a 45-day window to either sign up with Junara, move to an alternative email provider, or close their account. "To support users through this transition, all current Virgin Media customers wishing to move to Junara will receive their first year of service free of charge, with additional support available for those who need it."

metadata.title: 'Do not eat' warning in place for Waitrose shoppers as supermarket issues recall
metadata.contentSnippet: Waitrose has recalled two doughnut five-packs over undeclared soya. Check the best-before dates and how to get a refund.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Do not eat' warning in place for Waitrose shoppers as supermarket issues recall
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Waitrose has recalled two types of doughnuts because they contain soya not declared on the label. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has warned that the products could pose a health risk to anyone with an allergy to soya. The alert applies to England, Scotland and Wales. The affected products are Waitrose & Partners Sweet, Fluffy, Golden Ring Doughnuts 5's and Waitrose & Partners Jammy, Messy, Squidgy Doughnuts 5's. Tuesday 10 November - Waitrose & Partners recalls various Waitrose & Partners Doughnuts 5’s because of undeclared soya #FoodAllergy https://t.co/daUpmhxwL3 https://t.co/eFbF2SVY8L — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) November 10, 2026 Both are sold in packs of five, with best-before dates of November 10 and November 11 included in the recall. The FSA advises anyone who has bought the affected doughnuts and has an allergy to soya not to eat them. Instead, they should return the products to the store where they were bought for a full refund. A receipt is not required. For more information, shoppers can contact Waitrose Customer Care on 0800 188 884 and select option 4. Waitrose has contacted allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall, according to the FSA. An FSA spokesman said: "Waitrose & Partners are recalling the above products from customers and has contacted the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. "These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. "If you have bought the above products and have an allergy to soya do not eat them. Instead return them to the store from where they were bought for a full refund. No receipt required. For more information, please contact: Waitrose Customer Care 0800 188 884, option 4." If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

metadata.title: DWP starts bank checks on benefit claimants – what officials can now see
metadata.contentSnippet: The DWP has issued its first notice under new bank check powers. Find out which three benefits are affected and what banks can share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP starts bank checks on benefit claimants – what officials can now see
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed it has issued its first notice requiring banks to check accounts linked to benefit payments, marking the start of a major new crackdown on fraud and incorrect claims. The new powers mean banks and other financial institutions must check certain accounts against information supplied by the DWP to help establish whether people are still entitled to the benefits they receive. The measure could affect people claiming Universal Credit, Pension Credit and New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA), with the Government estimating it will save taxpayers £1.2billion over five years. Work and Pensions Minister Lilian Greenwood confirmed the first eligibility verification notice had been issued in a written statement to Parliament on October 26, explaining: "I am informing the House that the Department for Work and Pensions has issued the first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025, which amends the Social Security Administration Act 1992." The checks are designed to identify potential problems with benefit entitlement, particularly where someone may have more savings than the rules allow or has spent too long abroad. However, the DWP has stressed that the new powers do not give officials unrestricted access to people's bank accounts. Banks cannot hand over full statements or details of everyday spending, and a flag does not automatically mean someone has committed fraud or will lose their benefits - the full details are clarified here . The Eligibility Verification Measure (EVM) applies to three benefits: Under the system, the DWP sends banks and other financial institutions information known as 'eligibility indicators'. These are based on benefit rules relating to a claimant's capital, such as savings, and the amount of time they have spent abroad. Financial institutions then check the information they hold on accounts receiving specified DWP benefit payments. If an account meets one of the indicators, the bank must share limited information with the department. The checks can also cover linked accounts and joint accounts. The account does not necessarily have to belong to the person claiming the benefit – it could belong to someone else if it is linked to the account receiving the payment. The new powers do not give the DWP direct access to people's online banking or allow officials to monitor accounts in real time. Banks and financial institutions can share limited information if an eligibility indicator is met. This can include: However, banks cannot share full bank statements, details of individual transactions, how someone spends their money or the specific locations where transactions took place. They are also banned from sharing sensitive personal information about a person's background, such as political opinions or religious beliefs. Financial institutions could face fines if they disclose information they are not permitted to share. Today we discussed a new Bill to crack down on fraud. It's fair enough to go after those ripping off public money, but one section of the Bill has become a vehicle for bank spying powers, mandated by the DWP targetting benefit claimants. These new eligibility verification powers allow suspicionless surveillance - not a good precedent - and needs to be challenged, however much taxpayers money we're told mass financial monitoring will recoup. — Claire Fox (@Fox_Claire) May 15, 2025 A bank flag does not automatically mean someone has committed benefit fraud or will lose their payments. The information is intended to act as a prompt for the DWP to carry out further checks, rather than proof that someone has done something wrong. In her statement to Parliament, Ms Greenwood said: "The information received will act only as a prompt for further checks." She added: "Information received through EVM will not, in isolation, imply that a person is guilty of any wrongdoing or that their benefit entitlement will change." If information supplied by a bank suggests someone might be receiving an incorrect benefit payment, the DWP will review their claim. It could find that they are no longer eligible or that the amount they receive is wrong. The department may then contact the claimant to ask questions or request further information to establish whether they are still entitled to the benefit. The minister said: "DWP will have regard to all information relevant to a benefit decision, including information that was not obtained through EVM. Decisions will continue to be made by trained departmental staff through established processes." This means any decision about benefit entitlement or payments will be made by DWP staff, rather than automatically following information received from a bank. The department says it will contact people through their Universal Credit online journal if they have one. Those without an online account may be contacted by phone, letter or text message. Claimants are advised to respond as soon as possible to avoid their payments being delayed or stopped. Anyone who disagrees with a decision can ask the DWP to look at it again through a process known as a mandatory reconsideration. The new guidance also reminds claimants that they must keep the DWP informed if their circumstances change. This is particularly important for people whose benefit entitlement is affected by savings, income or time spent abroad. Changes that should be reported include: The DWP warns that failing to report a change promptly could mean someone receives too much benefit and has to repay the money. People who provide incorrect or incomplete information, or fail to report a change, could also face prosecution or a fine. If a claimant is unsure whether a change affects their payments, they should check the eligibility rules for the benefit they receive or contact the relevant DWP office. In her October 26 statement, Ms Greenwood told MPs that the department had issued its first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025. She said: "This marks an important step in the Department’s use of data to assist with identifying and preventing fraud and error, correcting inaccurate benefit payments sooner and helping prevent avoidable debt." Recommended reading: The minister said the measure was expected to save taxpayers £1.2billion over the next five years. She added that it would help ensure people received the support they were entitled to while protecting public money and addressing suspected fraud. The department will initially introduce the system through a controlled test-and-learn phase, allowing it to assess how it works before expanding its use. We're closing a loophole in Universal Credit Serious offenders detained for hospital treatment will no longer receive benefits while their living costs are being met by the NHS Watch Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden discuss the changes on @GMB https://t.co/ibm9VjDQ1w — Department for Work and Pensions (@DWPgovuk) October 20, 2026 Ms Greenwood said this would allow the DWP to assess "systems, data quality, operational impacts and customer outcomes" before the measure was scaled up. The Government says safeguards have been built into the legislation and a statutory code of practice, which sets out how the powers can be used and how personal information must be protected. Ms Greenwood told Parliament: "The measure contains a number of clear and vital safeguards."

metadata.title: DWP powers to check bank accounts limited to these 3 pensions and benefits
metadata.contentSnippet: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) can now have the bank accounts of millions of claimants on three key benefits checked under new government powers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP powers to check bank accounts limited to these 3 pensions and benefits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) can now have the bank accounts of millions of pensioners and benefit claimants checked under new government powers. This is part of controversial new benefit fraud rules, with powers created by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Bill. The new rules state: "The Government will begin implementing the Bill measures from 2026". At the moment, claimants on three types of pensions and benefit payments can have their bank accounts checked in this way. "This power can only be used to obtain information on accounts that receive a specified DWP benefit, and any accounts linked to that benefit receiving account if they match the eligibility indicators set by DWP," says the DWP’s Eligibility Verification powers in the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Bill information. The DWP adds: "The measure will initially focus on benefits where incorrect payments are currently highest, these are: "Other benefits could be added with the approval of Parliament in the future through affirmative regulations." State Pension is explicitly excluded from this power and cannot be added by regulations. According to information issued by the DWP, it will have the "power to require banks and other financial institutions to provide information to help verify a claimant’s entitlement to benefits and identify incorrect payments. "Banks and other financial institutions will be required to look at the data they hold on accounts in receipt of a specified DWP benefit payment and match these accounts to specific eligibility indicators determined by DWP (and defined within an Eligibility Verification Notice) and highlight where the criteria have been met." Discussing the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Bill - in rooting out benefit fraud (AND OVERPAYMENT ERROR), 'eligibility verification notices' amount to what @BigBrotherWatch call bank spying powers. I argued that, at the very least, those flagged up have a right… pic.twitter.com/ecrUl3eAsb — Claire Fox (@Fox_Claire) October 25, 2025 No, the rules are clear on this. Banks can only share limited information in response to an Eligibility Verification Notice, for example: They could receive a penalty for oversharing information, such as transaction information. The DWP also adds: "Any information shared through the Eligibility Verification Measure will not be shared on the presumption or suspicion that anyone is guilty of any offence." It gives the example of, for Universal Credit, an individual cannot hold more than £16,000 in savings and remain eligible for Universal Credit, "unless this capital is a result of a specified exception." There's a full list of those exceptions here. Recommended reading: "Where there are further inquiries or investigations, DWP will lead this, as it does now. "A human will always be involved in any decision taken afterwards which may affect benefit awards or eligibility, as they are now." They are keen to stress that this will not be done by AI tools. It will also be a gradual process: "DWP will be gradually rolling out the use of the Eligibility Verification Measure in a test and learn environment to allow for sufficient time for business to establish best processes." When fully rolled out the Department estimates that DWP will identify between 50,000 and 100,000 overpayments as a result of the measure each year.

metadata.title: The rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire’s fens, wetlands and waterways shelter some of Britain’s rarest wildlife including otters, bitterns, cranes and newts.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire’s fens, wetlands and waterways are home to some very unusual species of wildlife. If you're an avid birdwatcher, an aspiring lepidopterist or simply an animal lover, you'll want to keep a look out for these amazing creatures. So without further ado, here are some of the rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire. Otters have made a remarkable comeback in Cambridgeshire after once being driven close to extinction by pollution and habitat loss. They are now regularly spotted along the River Great Ouse, the River Cam and waterways such as Fen Drayton Lakes. Footage from Cambridge City Council shows an otter caught on camera at Logan's Meadow Local Nature Reserve. The UK's biggest and rarest newt is widespread across lowland England, particularly in wetlands. It has spotted flanks, a striking, orange belly, warty skin and is almost black in colour. The great crested newt is common in wetland environments (Image: Peter Hagger) The UK's tallest bird, standing at an impressive four feet, is instantly recognisable but disappeared from Britain for centuries. When a trio of migrating birds were blown off course in 1979, ending up in Norfolk, reintroduction projects began and there are now around 160 in Britain. If you're lucky, you can spot them in the Cambridgeshire Fens. Cambridgeshire’s wetland habitats are important for the bittern, a secretive heron whose distinctive booming call can be heard during spring and summer. Once extinct in the UK as a breeding species, its numbers have recovered through habitat restoration projects. According to the RSPB, the species is now thriving at the Ouse Fen nature reserve. A bittern in open flight (Image: Nigel Sprowell) According to the Essex Wildlife Trust, the East of England is the only place in Britain where water vole populations are increasing. However, they are under serious threat from habitat loss by the American mink. It can be distinguished from the brown rat by its furry tail and rounded nose.

Events included the annual procession and service in St Neots, alongside the Polish Remembrance Service at St Neots Cemetery and services in Eaton Socon and Eynesbury. The band of the 2500 St Neots Squadron RAF Air Cadets led the main procession, with its musicians helping to create a fitting and respectful atmosphere. The council said the strong turnout demonstrated the continuing importance of remembrance and the community's commitment to honouring those who served. A spokesman for St Neots Town Council added: “We will remember them.” Remembrance - Cadets with drums and flags during the St Neots remembrance procession (Image: St Neots Town Council) Parade - Scouts take part in the remembrance procession in St Neots (Image: St Neots Town Council) Special - A young flag bearer joins the St Neots remembrance gathering (Image: St Neots Town Council) Poppy - The St Neots remembrance procession (Image: St Neots Town Council) Commemorations - Attendees stand with a wreath (Image: St Neots Town Council) Military - Standards are held during an outdoor remembrance ceremony in St Neots (Image: St Neots Town Council) Poignant - A bugler plays during the remembrance ceremony (Image: St Neots Town Council) Tribute - A salute at the war memorial (Image: St Neots Town Council) Respect - A cadet holds a Union flag (Image: St Neots Town Council) Ceremony - Scouts salute beside wreaths (Image: St Neots Town Council) Reflect - Flowers are placed beside graves during the cemetery remembrance ceremony (Image: St Neots Town Council) Cemetery - A wreath is laid at a grave (Image: St Neots Town Council) United - Flag bearers attend the cemetery remembrance commemoration (Image: St Neots Town Council)

metadata.title: Care professional wins award for helping service user gain independence
metadata.contentSnippet: Care professionals have been honoured in Ely at an awards ceremony held in memory of a dedicated colleague.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Care professional wins award for helping service user gain independence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Care professionals have been honoured in Ely at an awards ceremony held in memory of a dedicated colleague. The third annual Kerry Care Awards, hosted by the St Ives-based Caring Together Charity, took place at Ely City Golf Club and celebrate outstanding members of the charity’s homecare team. The awards are named in honour of Kerry Giles-Brown, a care professional who worked with the charity for more than 30 years and died of cancer in 2024. Francis Burkitt, High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire, said: "I'm delighted to have been here to help Caring Together Charity celebrate the memory of Kerry and the amazing contribution she made to so many people for so many years. "Many congratulations to the winners, but every nominee deserves recognition for all they do. "These awards are a fitting tribute to Kerry, who was so dedicated to caring for others." The ceremony was attended by the High Sheriff, Mayor of Ely councillor Rebecca Dennes, Kerry’s husband Steven, and other family members, friends, and Caring Together Charity staff, volunteers and trustees. Kerry’s daughter Megan selected the winners from a list of nominees and presented the awards. First place went to Lynsey Matsell for her patient support of a service user with additional needs, helping them overcome anxiety and achieve greater independence. Megan Watson was named runner-up for the trust and confidence she inspires in service users and families through her kindness and professionalism. Third place went to Emily Shepherd, who was recognised for her compassion, positivity, and willingness to learn as someone new to the care profession. Lisa Downs, head of care at Caring Together Charity, said: "Kerry was an incredible person who was passionate about the care profession, and we want these awards to continue to be a fitting legacy to her. "Congratulations to Lynsey on winning the 2026 Kerry Care Award. "She is truly an asset to Caring Together and thoroughly deserves this recognition."

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire businesses urged to create new opportunities for young people
metadata.contentSnippet: Businesses across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough are being urged to offer apprenticeships and work experience through a new campaign

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire businesses urged to create new opportunities for young people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough are being urged to offer apprenticeships and work experience through a new campaign. Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce will launch its Opportunity Pledge at the CambsB2B South event on Thursday, November 12. Employers attending the event will be invited to make a commitment on a Pledge Wall, with T Level industry placements and internships among the opportunities they can offer. The campaign is open to businesses of all sizes and aims to encourage those that have not offered such opportunities before to take their first steps. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive officer of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "Businesses across our region are already experiencing the consequences of skills shortages, and the evidence tells us that developing the next generation of talent must be a priority if we are to sustain economic growth. "We want employers to consider what they can offer, whether that's taking on an apprentice, providing a T Level industry placement or giving someone their first meaningful experience of the workplace." Opportunity - Attendees greet each other during a conference session (Image: Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce) The initiative comes as the 2026 to 2029 Cambridgeshire and Peterborough LSIP highlights challenges facing the region's future workforce. The report identifies that 86 per cent of future workforce demand will be driven by the need to replace existing workers. Those making a pledge will be recognised as Future Skills Champions, with their commitments displayed on the Opportunity Pledge Wall and mirrored online through the chamber's website. Participating employers will receive a digital badge and may have opportunities to feature in future campaign activity and case studies. The campaign will continue beyond CambsB2B South, with businesses able to submit pledges through the chamber's website. Ms Horobin added: "For businesses that have never done this before, we want to demonstrate that there is support available to help them take that first step. "You don't have to be a large employer to make a meaningful contribution. "As the organisation representing the employer voice through the Local Skills Improvement Plan, I would encourage every business attending CambsB2B South to visit the Pledge Wall and consider the role they can play in developing our future workforce." The event takes place at TWI Ltd, Granta Park, Great Abington, Cambridge, and is free to attend, but advance registration is required through the chamber's CambsB2B South page.

metadata.title: Frank’s Farm launches cookery classes in converted grain store
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridgeshire farm has launched its first cookery classes in a converted grain store.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Frank’s Farm launches cookery classes in converted grain store
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire farm has launched its first cookery classes in a converted grain store. Frank’s Farm, in Elsworth, is offering hands-on sessions led by chef Julia Quy, covering dishes from Thai curries to festive canapés and seafood. The classes are held in a state of the art, converted grain store. Ms Quy said: "We believe cooking should be joyful, a little messy and always delicious. "Whether you’re a total beginner or just looking to level up your kitchen game, our hands-on classes bring people together over good food, good laughs and the occasional glass of wine. "There are no stuffy techniques, no intimidating jargon – just great ingredients, a friendly environment, beautiful surroundings and recipes you’ll actually want to make again at home." The first programme runs from November 2026 to March 2027, with sessions including A Taste of Thailand, Saturday Brunch, Festive Canapés, The Secrets of Indian Curry and Beef Wellington Masterclass. Classes also explore Lebanese, Caribbean and Greek Cuisine, as well as choux pastry, seafood and French macarons. A special cupcake-making day is planned for children during the Easter holidays. Menus may change based on class size and the availability of seasonal ingredients. For more details and to book, visit https://franks.farm/product-category/courses/.

metadata.title: Veteran with 40 years’ service attends Huntingdon Remembrance memorial
metadata.contentSnippet: A veteran who lives at Bayleaf Care Home with more than 40 years of military service was proud to take part in the Huntingdon memorial service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Veteran with 40 years’ service attends Huntingdon Remembrance memorial
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A veteran with more than 40 years of military service was proud to take part in the Huntingdon memorial service this Remembrance Sunday. John Evans, known to many as "Basha," now lives at Bayleaf Care Home in Huntingdon and has shared his story in the days surrounding Remembrance Sunday. Mr Evans spent a period of his life living locally in Papworth and served in the Special Forces and the Parachute Regiment during his long military career. A spokesperson for Bayleaf Care Home said: "In the days leading up to Remembrance Sunday, John had been a little quieter than usual. "But following the memorial service in Huntingdon, we saw a different side of him. "Proudly dressed, with his medals taking pride of place, it was clear just how much the occasion meant to him. John Evans is better known to many as Basha (Image: Bayleaf Care Home) "For those of us getting to know John, discovering more about his past has been a privilege." In the week following Remembrance Sunday, Mr Evans began to open up about his past, sharing stories of a life that took him far beyond the streets of Papworth. He also spoke with those around him about his love of model aircraft and woodwork, and the importance of friendship. John remains in contact with some of the men he served alongside, and Bayleaf Care Home plans to host around 10 of them at an upcoming veteran lunch. John lived in Papworth for a large portion of his life (Image: Bayleaf Care Home) The spokesperson said: "At Bayleaf, we believe that every person has a story worth telling. "The experiences, achievements, friendships and memories that make someone who they are should never be lost or overlooked. "This Remembrance Sunday reminded us that behind every medal is a person, behind every uniform is a lifetime of memories, and behind every story is someone worth taking the time to know."

metadata.title: Former Cambs police officer turned up to work 'smelling strongly of alcohol'
metadata.contentSnippet: Former Cambridgeshire police officer Ciaron Hickey would have been dismissed for gross misconduct after arriving at training smelling of alcohol, a hearing found.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambs police officer turned up to work 'smelling strongly of alcohol'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A police officer who turned up to work smelling of alcohol would have been sacked for gross misconduct, a hearing found. Former PC Ciaron Hickey, who served with Cambridgeshire Constabulary, attended a first aid refresher course at force headquarters on September 10, 2025. He arrived late, explaining that this was due to him mistakenly attending a local police station. A member of the Public and Personal Safety Training Team (PPST) detected the smell of alcohol on Mr Hickey’s breath after having a brief conversation with him outside the classroom. The PPST trainer confirmed he smelt of alcohol and reported it to the sergeant present. Mr Hickey was removed from the classroom and later admitted drinking alcohol the night before. A preliminary breath test showed 18 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath. A second test an hour later showed 9 micrograms, and he was taken home. At the time of the incident, he was already under a written warning for a similar offence, having reported for duty on September 11, 2024, with excess alcohol in his system. A police misconduct hearing held at Lysander House in Bedfordshire on October 21 concluded that Mr Hickey’s actions amounted to gross misconduct. The panel found that he breached standards on fitness for duty, orders and instructions, and discreditable conduct by attending training "smelling strongly of alcohol". Mr Hickey resigned from the force on October 19, 2026, did not attend the hearing and was not represented. His federation representative confirmed he did not wish to engage with the proceedings. The panel accepted his early admission and co-operation with the investigation as mitigating factors, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his actions. The report stated: "The panel considered that the proven conduct was so serious as to justify dismissal and even more so, when considered together with the live written warning for similar conduct." The panel also considered the "personal difficulties" he was experiencing, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his conduct. As Mr Hickey was no longer a serving officer at the time of the hearing, the panel could not impose a formal disciplinary sanction. Instead, it recorded that he would have been dismissed without notice had he still been employed. ACC Vaughan Lukey chaired the misconduct panel, alongside independent members Davide Corbino and Bryan McAlley. David Tyme served as the legally qualified person.

Drug dealer jailed after police find £24,000 heroin and crack cocaine stash
metadata.contentSnippet: A drug dealer has been jailed after police stopped him in Cambridge and later found a stash of £24,000 worth of heroin and crack cocaine.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drug dealer jailed after police find £24,000 heroin and crack cocaine stash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drug dealer has been jailed after police stopped him in Cambridgeshire and later found a stash of £24,000 worth of heroin and crack cocaine. Robert St Paul, 27, was intercepted alongside Brooklyn Coburn, 27, after police stopped a grey Subaru on Cromwell Road, Cambridge, on December 10. The force had received intelligence linking the vehicle to drug dealing. Officers searched Coburn, the driver, and found crack cocaine and heroin concealed in his underwear. St Paul, who was a passenger in the vehicle, was found with a mobile phone, while two more phones and cash were discovered in the car. Police then searched both men’s homes as part of the drug investigation. Police found cash at Coburn’s Woking address and heroin and crack cocaine worth £24,000 at St Paul’s flat in Hall Road, Newham. Police found a stash of heroin and crack cocaine worth £24,000 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) At Cambridge Crown Court on November 9, Coburn, of Beckenham, London, was given a two-year prison sentence suspended for two years. He must also complete 180 hours of unpaid work. St Paul, of no fixed address, was jailed for 40 months on May 5 after pleading guilty to the same offences. Police intercepted St Paul in Cambridge (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable Ben Bowen, who investigated, said: "Cambridgeshire is not a soft target for drug dealers. "If you travel into our county to sell drugs, we will use intelligence to identify you, stop you and put you before the courts. "Drug dealing causes misery in our communities and often goes hand-in-hand with violence, exploitation and other crime. "We will continue to target those responsible and disrupt the supply of Class A drugs."

David Walliams tried to block publication of sexual misconduct allegations
metadata.contentSnippet: Multiple women have accused David Walliams of sexually inappropriate behaviour and grooming, which he denies

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: David Walliams tried to block publication of sexual misconduct allegations
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: David Walliams has been named as the celebrity who tried to block publication of his identity amid allegations of “inappropriate sexual activities” with girls and young women. Multiple women have accused David Walliams of sexually inappropriate behaviour and grooming including when they were teenagers, according to an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Walliams denies all allegations against him. A joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian alleges Walliams preyed on teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. Multiple women accuse Walliams of “grooming” them as teenagers, while another described her alleged encounter with Walliams as “sexual assault”. Walliams is also accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Responding to the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams denied all allegations against him. He said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with... I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. “And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did... “I am not a sexual predator... I have not broken the law... I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Gavin Millar KC said that reporters from the media organisations had spoken to more than 100 people, including more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts as well as Walliams’ friends and colleagues. Walliams’ lawyers said that he had initially attempted suicide after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his reply to the allegations, because of “long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media”. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. Walliams’ book publisher HarperCollins dropped him in December 2025, after an investigation into allegations he had “harassed” young women, which Walliams strongly denied. Earlier this month, theme park Alton Towers permanently closed its World Of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by the books. Walliams left Britain’s Got Talent in 2022 after he apologised for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants during filming breaks in January 2020 at the London Palladium. In 2023, Britain’s Got Talent producer Fremantle apologised and reached an “amicable resolution” with Walliams after the remarks he made while on the show were leaked.

metadata.title: Workers over 21 given £910 cash boost confirms Andy Burnham
metadata.contentSnippet: Millions of workers are in line for a £910 pay rise next April, with Andy Burnham's Government confirming a 3.9% increase to the National Living Wage.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Workers over 21 given £910 cash boost confirms Andy Burnham
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of workers are in line for a pay rise next April, with Andy Burnham's Government confirming a 3.9% increase to the National Living Wage. The increase means people aged 21 and over who work full-time on the minimum rate will see their gross annual earnings rise by £910 from April 1, 2027, according to HM Treasury. The National Living Wage will increase from £12.71 to £13.21 an hour, with around 2.3 million workers across the UK expected to benefit from the changes. Younger workers will also receive a boost, with the National Minimum Wage for those aged 18 to 20 rising by the same percentage. Their hourly rate will increase from £10.85 to £11.27, also from April 1. The 3.9% increase is higher than the latest Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation figure, which stood at 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026. Confirming the changes, HM Treasury said: "To support low-paid workers across the UK, the government is raising the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wages, which is expected to benefit around 2.3 million workers. "On 1 April 2027, the National Living Wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 per hour, equivalent to an increase of £910 in the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker on the National Living Wage. The National Minimum Wage for 18- to 20-year-olds will also increase by 3.9% to £11.27 per hour. "By accepting the Low Pay Commission's recommendations in full this year, the government is ensuring workers are rewarded fairly for their work, while protecting jobs, backing businesses, and strengthening the conditions for economic growth." The £910 annual increase applies to someone aged 21 or over working full-time on the National Living Wage. It is a rise in gross earnings, meaning the figure is before Income Tax and National Insurance deductions. The new hourly rate of £13.21 will apply from April 1, 2027. Workers aged 18 to 20 will see their minimum hourly pay increase by 42p, from £10.85 to £11.27. The latest increase also marks a change in the pace of pay rises for younger workers. Since Labour returned to power in 2024, the National Minimum Wage for 18 to 20-year-olds has increased by 26%. The 2027 rise brings their increase into line with the percentage increase for workers aged 21 and over, rather than giving younger workers a larger proportional uplift. The 3.9% increase is above the latest CPI inflation rate of 3.5%, recorded by the Office for National Statistics in the year to September 2026. Recommended reading: The Low Pay Commission (LPC), which advises the Government on minimum wage rates, had previously said the National Living Wage would need to rise by around 3.7% in 2027 to reach £13.18 an hour, keeping pace with its expectations for average pay growth. However, in March, it changed the LPC's remit to give it more scope to consider labour market conditions when setting the minimum wage for 18 to 20-year-olds. The new rates will take effect on April 1, 2027.

metadata.contentSnippet: Around 1,600 people gathered in St Ives for Remembrance Sunday, with 350 parade participants, veterans, cadets and community groups honouring the Armed Forces.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Around 1,600 gather in St Ives for Remembrance Sunday tribute
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Around 1,600 people gathered in St Ives to pay tribute to those who served in the Armed Forces on Remembrance Sunday. A parade of more than 350 participants marched through the town, led by the Corps of Drums, in a show of unity and respect. Veterans, cadet forces, youth organisations, civic representatives, emergency services, and community groups all took part in the moving ceremony. St Ives Town Council said: "St Ives Town Council would like to express its sincere thanks to everyone who took part in the commemorations, including those who marched, carried standards, volunteered, supported the event and attended the service." Among those in attendance were the Deputy Lieutenant for Cambridgeshire, Mrs Jennifer Crompton DL, representatives of 42 Engineer Regiment, and members of the United States Visiting Forces. The service was led by Canon Simon Kershaw, with the Mayor of St Ives, Councillor Alexander Thompson, delivering a heartfelt address. The Act of Remembrance and the two-minute silence were observed with dignity and respect. Raised standards and the scale of attendance reflected the community’s ongoing commitment to honouring those who gave their lives in service to their country.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 film and television locations you can visit in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Famous film and TV locations are closer than you might think. Cambridgeshire has quietly become a star of the screen, with its historic streets, rural villages, and grand buildings providing the backdrop to some of cinema and television’s most memorable moments. From Netflix’s The Crown to ITV’s Grantchester, the county has featured in a growing list of productions, attracting fans keen to follow in their favourite characters’ footsteps. Here are some of Cambridgeshire’s best-known filming locations. Wansford Station and the Nene Valley Railway near Peterborough has been used for not one, but two James Bond films. (Image: Nene Valley Railway) Ely Cathedral is one of Cambridgeshire’s most spectacular filming locations. The cathedral stood in for Westminster Abbey in Netflix’s The Crown, including during wedding and coronation scenes. More recently, Bradley Cooper filmed one of Maestro’s most memorable scenes inside the cathedral. Cooper played legendary American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, and directed and co-wrote the film. For one of the film's major scenes, Cooper recreated Bernstein's celebrated 1973 performance of Gustav Mahler's Resurrection Symphony at Ely Cathedral. The sequence was filmed inside the cathedral with a live orchestra, choir and extras, and much of it unfolds in a single six-minute take. Visitors to Ely can walk through the cathedral used for one of the Oscar-nominated film’s major musical sequences. The Green Man n Grantchester is used by ITV for its detective drama Granchester starring Robson Green. (Image: Google Street View) Few places in Cambridgeshire are as closely linked to a television programme as Grantchester is to Grantchester. The picturesque village provides the setting for ITV’s detective drama of the same name, which uses several real locations. Fans can explore the village’s buildings and landscapes, which regularly appear on screen alongside Robson Green, Tessa Peake-Jones, Kacey Ainsworth and Al Weaver. One particularly recognisable location is the Church of St Andrew and St Mary, which has appeared in Grantchester as the village church and churchyard. Grantchester Meadows is another location visitors can enjoy for free. The meadows beside the River Cam feature in Grantchester and offer fans a taste of the countryside behind the programme. The meadows are also worth visiting in their own right, especially for fans who want to combine screen tourism with a riverside walk. Fans can stop for a drink at The Green Man pub, frequented by Geordie and his colleagues in the show. It lets visitors step inside a genuine screen location instead of viewing it from the road. Wisbech offers a very different look, with the Fenland town’s historic streets appearing in films and television productions. Peckover House in Wisbech has been used for films including Dean Spanley starring Peter O'Toole. (Image: Image: National Trust Images Jemma Finch) The town is known for its Georgian architecture, particularly North Brink, which overlooks the River Nene and has an impressive row of period properties. The National Trust’s Peckover House, a Georgian merchant’s home dating from 1722, also stands on North Brink. Productions filmed in Wisbech include the 1994 television adaptation of Martin Chuzzlewit, David Copperfield from 1999 to 2000 and the 2008 film Dean Spanley. The 2022 independent film Wild Bones was also filmed in Wisbech. Peter O’Toole filmed Dean Spanley in Wisbech in 2007 alongside Sam Neill, Bryan Brown and Jeremy Northam, with Peckover House and Wisbech Castle among the locations used. Visitors can explore much of the town’s Georgian heritage on foot, especially around North Brink, South Brink and the River Nene. James Bond fans have good reason to visit Peterborough: the area provided locations for two 007 films. The Nene Valley Railway featured in 1983’s Octopussy, starring Roger Moore as James Bond. Wansford Station became the fictional Karl Marx Stadt station, while filming also took place around Orton Mere and Ferry Meadows. The Bond franchise returned to Peterborough for 1995’s GoldenEye, Pierce Brosnan’s first 007 film. The Nene Valley Railway hosted action scenes involving the film’s imposing Russian armoured train. The former British Sugar factory at Woodston also featured in GoldenEye. Part of the site became a Russian rail depot, and Peterborough provided the backdrop for the tank chase’s finale. The former industrial site has been redeveloped, but the Nene Valley Railway remains open, so Bond fans can still visit a location featured in two 007 films. Just outside Cambridgeshire’s modern boundary, Burghley House is one of the wider region’s most impressive filming locations. Burghley House, just over the border near Stamford was used for the 2005 series of Pride and Prejudice among other films and TV series. (Image: Burghley House) The Elizabethan mansion is best known for appearing as Rosings Park, Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s imposing home, in the 2005 adaptation of Pride & Prejudice. The house and grounds are open to visitors during the visitor season, giving film fans a chance to see the grand setting for themselves. From Bradley Cooper conducting inside Ely Cathedral to James Bond racing through Peterborough, Cambridgeshire has made a striking mark on the big and small screens. And with many of the locations open to the public, film and television fans do not have to settle for watching them from the sofa.

metadata.title: Woman with MS delivers 16,000-signature petition calling for fairer PIP assessments
metadata.contentSnippet: A woman living with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Huntingdon has delivered a petition signed by over 16,000 people to the UK Government.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman with MS delivers 16,000-signature petition calling for fairer PIP assessments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman living with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Huntingdon has delivered a petition signed by over 16,000 people to the UK Government. The petition calls on the government to make Personal Independence Payment (PIP) fairer for people with MS. It was delivered on November 3 by 56-year-old Sharon Docherty, who has secondary progressive MS. She was joined by Janis Winehouse, Amy Winehouse’s mother and also living with MS, and Neil Duncan Jordan MP. Sharon said: "During my assessment, it appeared the assessor had not read any of the medical evidence I'd submitted. "It also felt like the questions they asked did not allow me to explain the full nuances of living with a condition like MS." MP Neil Duncan-Jordan PIP hand in (Image: Sharon Docherty) The petition was organised by the MS Society to coincide with the government’s review into PIP, the Timms Review, which will be published later this month. Sharon worked closely with the charity to develop the campaign. More than 150,000 people in the UK live with MS, including an estimated 1,900 in Cambridgeshire. The neurological condition affects the brain and spinal cord and can cause a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that often fluctuate or remain invisible to others. PIP is designed to help disabled people cover the extra costs of living independently, but the assessment process has been widely criticised as "rigid" and not reflective of variable conditions like MS. Sharon said: "At times, the system can feel as though it is designed to discourage people from applying rather than support those who need help." She said receiving PIP has allowed her to engage in activities recommended by her therapist, but she's due to be reassessed in five years' time despite having a progressive condition. The MS Society is calling for a more flexible, person-centred approach to PIP, including lifetime awards for people with long-term, progressive conditions and an end to unnecessary reassessments.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire Constabulary honours officers, staff and volunteers at awards ceremony
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Constabulary honoured officers, staff and volunteers at an awards ceremony.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire Constabulary honours officers, staff and volunteers at awards ceremony
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: POLICE officers, staff and volunteers have been honoured for making a difference in Cambridgeshire. Cambridgeshire Constabulary held its annual awards at Burgess Hall in St Ives on Friday, November 6, recognising exceptional contributions and courageous service. The awards recognised achievements ranging from tackling organised crime to supporting young people and making communities safer. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: "Every day I see outstanding and inspiring work by officers, staff and volunteers and I am delighted to recognise each and every one of them for the challenging and often thankless tasks they do to keep the people of the county safe. "Working as a team is key to our success and this ceremony is an important opportunity for us to celebrate that, showing our appreciation for all the hard work and professionalism displayed throughout the past year. "The evening is also a celebration of the values and principles that unite us as an organisation. "Our vision is simple – to create a safer Cambridgeshire, and every finalist has played a part in delivering our mission to prevent harm, reduce and solve crime, and build trust and confidence in policing." Commitment to Outstanding Leadership winner Inspector Edward McNeil (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Inspector Edward McNeil won the Commitment to Outstanding Leadership award for modernising resource management and advancing force priorities through inclusive leadership. Volunteer police cadet coordinator Alison Wicking was recognised for her commitment to safeguarding. Commitment to Safeguarding winner Alison Wicking (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) She regularly gives up her own time to support young people and make sure they feel included in the cadet programme. Inspector Luke Coulson was recognised for championing health and wellbeing. Commitment to Health and Wellbeing winner Inspector Luke Coulson (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) He turned the Copse Court tuck shop into a useful resource for officers working long shifts and raised money for team welfare activities. Tom Broad was named Cadet of the Year for his professionalism, leadership and positive influence on younger cadets. Cadet of the Year Tom Broad (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Leonard W Dunbar MBE was named Volunteer of the Year for his role in officer training. He brings scenarios to life through realistic role-play, helping student officers build key skills. Volunteer of the Year Leonard W Dunbar MBE (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Special Inspector Thomas Howard was named Special of the Year for his operational leadership and work on road safety and community projects. Special of the Year Thomas Howard (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) PCSO Ian Moll was recognised for tackling theft and anti-social behaviour while maintaining a visible presence in Peterborough city centre. PCSO of the Year winner Ian Moll (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Isla Harrison was named Student Officer of the Year after completing her portfolio in just over six months and impressing colleagues with her professionalism and willingness to learn. PC Chris Hobson was named Investigator of the Year for supporting vulnerable people and improving outcomes in mental health cases. Police Staff Employee of the Year Lee Eagle (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Detention officer Lee Eagle was named Police Staff Employee of the Year for his calm, compassionate approach in custody. PC Chris Ogden was named Police Officer of the Year. Police Officer of the Year Chris Ogden (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) He disrupted an organised drug network through intelligence-gathering and a determined investigation. The north and south spree offender teams won Team of the Year for managing repeat offenders and reducing harm through proactive partnership work. Unsung Hero Amanda Large (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Amanda Large was named Unsung Hero after more than 30 years supporting colleagues, volunteers and young people across the force. Grand Prix Employee of the Year Chris Ogden (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) PC Ogden also won the Grand Prix Employee of the Year award, chosen by the chief constable from the winners. The ceremony was supported by sponsors including Black Marble, Neville Special Projects, the Police Federation, The Garden, Willmott Dixon, Thrive, Little Piggy Catering, Mark Waller Ground Maintenance, Visav and Peterborough Positive.

metadata.title: Martin Lewis issues 'awful' energy bill warning as price cap set to jump by £276
metadata.contentSnippet: Martin Lewis warns energy bills could get worse before they improve, as the Ofgem price cap is forecast to rise by £276 in January 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis issues 'awful' energy bill warning as price cap set to jump by £276
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households struggling with energy bills that costs are likely to get worse before they get better, as millions of people face the 'awful' prospect of a sharp rise in January. On his X account, the Money Saving Expert founder said: "The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket." It comes as energy analysts predict the Ofgem price cap could jump by 16 per cent at the start of 2027, adding hundreds of pounds to the annual bill of a typical household. Experts at Cornwall Insight forecast that the cap will rise by £276, taking it from £1,723 to £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household from January 2027. The prospect of another increase will be particularly worrying for families heading into one of the coldest and most expensive periods of the year, when heating demand typically rises and daylight hours are shorter. There are also fears the increase could be even bigger if the conflict involving the US, Iran and Israel continues to disrupt energy markets and push up wholesale gas prices. The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket. PS Jan prediction is getting much more locked in as we're 85% through the 19 August to 17 November 2026 assessment period. April & July predictions are much more crystal ballgazing. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 3, 2026 There has been some positive news for households, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing a series of measures intended to ease pressure on energy bills. These include removing VAT from domestic energy bills, which is expected to save the average household around £45 to £50, and a £100 winter energy payment for around 20 million households living in Council Tax bands A to D. The Government has also confirmed plans to scrap gas standing charges, which are fixed daily fees households pay regardless of how much gas they use. Best to keep the heating on low all day? Does foil behind radiators work? Is now the time to fix? Got questions on energy bills, energy efficiency, solar panels & more, that's next week's @ITVMlshow. I'll be joined by specialist heat engineers so pls post questions by reply. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 6, 2026 However, Martin Lewis warned that consumers could have to wait until late 2027 or even January 2028 before the change takes effect. Chancellor John Healey said the Government would ask Ofgem to deliver the removal of the charges in 2027, or as soon as possible afterwards. Speaking about the timetable, Mr Lewis said: "The gas standing charge, on the price cap anyway, is to be scrapped in 2027. What does 2027 mean? Well, as it's part of the price cap, it definitely won't be before the 1st of October." The typical gas standing charge is currently around £108 a year for households paying by direct debit or prepayment meter. Under the planned changes, this fixed cost will be moved into the unit rate – the amount customers pay for each kilowatt-hour of gas they use. That means the reform will not automatically cut everyone's bill. Instead, households that use less gas should benefit, while those who use more could pay more. Mr Lewis said: "This isn't about saving money in totality. This is about a structural change and I've always argued that – for fairness – so that those low users who struggle at the moment to cut their bills because so much of it is about the standing charge, and I get so many messages about this, that won't happen anymore." He estimated that the change could add roughly 0.8p to 0.9p per kilowatt-hour to the gas unit rate, although he stressed this was only a rough calculation and the final figure would depend on energy prices at the time. He added: "What does it mean? Lower users will pay less, higher users will pay more. And actually, because there are quite a lot a low number of very high users and it's done on the mean average, it actually works out 60 per cent of people will pay less, 40 per cent of people will pay more." The Government estimates that around 60 per cent of account-holding households could save an average of £45 a year as a result of the change. In a statement, the Government said: "Tens of millions of households will no longer pay standing charges on their gas bills as the Government gives families more control over what they pay and some more breathing space. "A standing charge is a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill, regardless of how much gas has been used. A household could use no gas at all but still must pay the standing charge. "The Chancellor will announce an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after. "Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill." The Ofgem price cap currently stands at £1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel household paying by direct debit. This is a 3.6 per cent increase on the previous three-month period. The price cap sets the maximum rates suppliers can charge customers on standard variable tariffs for each unit of gas and electricity, as well as the daily standing charges. It is not a limit on the total amount a household can pay, meaning bills will be higher for those who use more energy. Cornwall Insight expects the cap to rise by 16 per cent in January 2027, reaching £1,999 a year – an increase of £276. The consultancy said: "The price cap is expected to rise by 16% compared to October, reaching £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household in January 2027, an increase of £276 and the largest rise since January 2023." It said the increase was largely being driven by escalating conflict in the Middle East, which continues to disrupt gas supplies in the UK and around the world. The consultancy added that EU gas storage stocks had fallen to their lowest September levels in 15 years, adding to pressure on the market. It also warned that some of the price increases had already been reflected in the calculation for January's cap. Cornwall Insight said: "Ofgem sets the wholesale part of the cap using prices from a fixed period known as the observation window. With that window for the January cap now nearly halfway through, the price rises seen in September are already locked in, making a January increase all but certain."

metadata.title: School praised for ‘courteous’ pupils and strong attendance by Ofsted inspectors
metadata.contentSnippet: A primary school in Brington has been praised for its community spirit and pupils’ behaviour after a recent Ofsted inspection.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: School praised for ‘courteous’ pupils and strong attendance by Ofsted inspectors
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school has been praised for its community spirit and pupils’ behaviour after a recent Ofsted inspection. Brington CofE Primary School, in Church Lane, Brington, received the report after inspectors visited on September 29 and 30. Ofsted rated attendance and behaviour as “strong”. Achievement, curriculum, teaching, early years, inclusion, leadership, governance, personal development and wellbeing met the “expected” standard. Kirsty Baish, headteacher, said: "I feel incredibly privileged to lead a school that means so much to me. "I want every child who walks through our doors to be happy, feel safe, be challenged academically and have the confidence to fulfil their potential. "I am incredibly proud of how far we have come, but we are not a school that stands still. "We have high aspirations for our children." The report described pupils as “courteous” and “respectful”. Older children looked after younger pupils and helped everyone feel included. Inspectors said pupils approached learning enthusiastically, helping create a “calm, inclusive and purposeful environment”. Pupils made good academic progress across a wide range of subjects and developed the knowledge and skills needed for their next stage of education. Ofsted singled out reading as a strength and said it was at the heart of the curriculum. The school’s approach to phonics and early reading was said to help pupils develop both confidence and fluency. The school says its motto, “Build each other up to be the best you can be”, sums up its aim of helping children support one another, believe in themselves and aim high. Children in the early years made a strong start, while pupils with special educational needs and disabilities were included across school life and given tailored support. Ofsted also praised the wider opportunities available to pupils, including sport, music, and leadership activities. Swimming was singled out as a particular strength, with the school’s on-site pool helping children develop water confidence and swimming skills. However, inspectors identified areas for improvement. Some lessons offered effective challenge and adaptations, but this was not consistent across subjects and year groups. Ofsted recommended that leaders improve the consistency of curriculum delivery to ensure all pupils, especially those needing adaptations or capable of greater challenge, could build securely on previous learning. The report also called for stronger leadership to ensure improvement work is properly assessed and changes are consistently embedded. Debra Beachus-Wells, chair of governors, said: "Brington isn't just a school; it's a whole community, one that is inclusive and welcoming to all pupils and parents. "Since Mrs Baish took on the headship in May 2025, she has achieved such positive improvements across the school. "The progress made is clear for everyone to see and is reflected in the recent Ofsted report. "The Governing Board is fully committed to continuing to work closely with Mrs Baish, the staff, pupils and parents to build on this success. "Together, we want to keep moving the school forward, making further improvements and ensuring Brington continues to be the fantastic school and community that we all know it can be. "We are proud of what has been achieved so far and excited about what we can accomplish together in the future." The report said overall absence was 3.9 per cent in 2025/26, compared with 5.1 per cent nationally. Persistent absence was 8.4 per cent, compared with 14.4 per cent nationally. Mrs Baish said: "This is a celebration of our whole school community – our wonderful children, dedicated staff, supportive governors and families. "We are proud of Brington, proud of our journey and excited about our future."

St Ivo golfer celebrates incredible season with back-to-back championship wins
metadata.contentSnippet: A talented young golfer who goes to St Ivo Academy has capped an outstanding season by successfully defending two major titles while competing against players from across the UK and Europe.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ivo golfer celebrates incredible season with back-to-back championship wins
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A talented young golfer has capped an outstanding season by successfully defending two major titles while competing against players from across the UK and Europe. St Ivo Academy pupil Harry Burgess retained both the Junior British Masters Championship and St Andrews WAGR World Series titles during a remarkable 2026 campaign. Harry has lowered his handicap to just 0.9 and travelled more than 30,000 miles for competitions across 11 counties and several countries. His season began with victory while representing St Ivo Academy at the Cambridgeshire Schools Championships, before he went on to represent Cambridgeshire at under-14, under-16 and under-18 level. The school has supported Harry’s development by allowing him to leave on Tuesday afternoons for intensive technical and fitness training. Trophy - Harry with European Tour legend Robert Rock (Image: Phil Burgess) One of his biggest successes came at The Belfry, where he successfully defended the Junior British Masters title on the famous Brabazon Course against young golfers from across the UK. Harry then travelled to St Andrews and retained his WAGR World Series title against competitors from across Europe. The 54-hole competition ended with one of his best rounds, as he carded a gross 69 and recorded an albatross on the par-five third hole. He also had a putt to complete the front nine in 29 shots, which would have equalled the course record. Titles - Harry with the Andy Finnigan Trophy (Image: Phil Burgess) His other achievements include becoming under-14 county champion and St Ives Junior Club Champion. He also secured three national tour titles and won the Andy Finnigan Trophy after recording a gross 66 at John O’Gaunt. Harry finished second in the National Tour Order of Merit and is now preparing for further competitions in Spain, Ireland, Wales and Scotland. He is also due to compete at the World Championships later in the year. Harry’s ambitions extend beyond his continuing junior career, with the youngster hoping eventually to combine his education with developing his golf overseas. After completing his studies at St Ivo Academy, he hopes to secure a golf scholarship in America and continue playing at the highest level possible.

metadata.title: Burglar jailed after stealing more than £2,000 worth of alcohol
metadata.contentSnippet: A burglar who targeted Cambridge properties and stole more than £2,000 worth of alcohol, including from Margaret’s Cambridge, has been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Burglar jailed after stealing more than £2,000 worth of alcohol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A burglar who "repeatedly targeted" Cambridgeshire properties and stole more than £2,000 worth of alcohol has been jailed. Darren Valentine, 35, of no fixed address, admitted three burglaries, five attempted burglaries, breaching a Criminal Behaviour Order and attempting to steal a car. On May 26, Valentine climbed into the rear garden of Margaret’s Cambridge on Chesterton Road and stole £400 worth of alcohol from its cellar. On August 29, he broke into a garage on Mariners Way in Chesterton and stole two bikes, an electric moped and £1,830 worth of alcohol. Between August 29 and 31, he tried to break into garages at five Capstan Close properties. On August 31, he got into another Capstan Close garage but left empty-handed. Darren Valentine repeatedly targeted Cambridgeshire properties in a string of break-ins (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Valentine was jailed for 20 months at Peterborough Crown Court on November 5. Detective Constable Ed Glasse, who investigated, said: "Valentine repeatedly targeted properties in Chesterton, stealing hundreds of pounds worth of items and trying to break into a number of other garages. “Burglary can have a significant impact on those affected and I hope this sentence provides some reassurance to the residents and businesses he targeted. “We will continue to pursue those responsible for burglary and put them before the courts.”

metadata.title: Face of drug dealer jailed after being caught with cocaine
metadata.contentSnippet: A drug dealer has been jailed after being caught with cocaine on Campkin Road in Cambridge and refusing to stop for police.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Face of drug dealer jailed after being caught with cocaine
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drug dealer has been jailed after being caught with cocaine in Cambridgeshire and refusing to stop for police. Police arrested Daniel Myftarago, 27, of Alder Walk, Ilford, Essex, in Cambridge on December 18, 2023. Neighbourhood Support Team officers spotted a red Mazda acting suspiciously on Campkin Road and found it was insured to people at two different addresses. When they attempted to stop the car, the driver failed to comply and continued driving until reaching a dead end on Somerset Close. Myftarago, who was a passenger in the vehicle, was searched by officers who found cocaine, two mobile phones, and £270 in cash. Daniel Myftarago was jailed for three years and ten months on November 6 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Following a four-day trial in September, he was found guilty of possession with intent to supply cocaine, being concerned in the supply of cocaine, and possession of criminal property. Myftarago was jailed for three years and 10 months at Huntingdon Law Courts on Friday, November 6. PC Jodie Skells, who investigated the case, said: "We will continue to target people like Myftarago who come into our county to deal drugs. "Drugs bring misery and associated violence to communities and will not be tolerated." If you suspect drug dealing where you live, report it to police online.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man died after being hit by a train between Huntingdon and Peterborough, British Transport Police confirmed in an update. The force were called at 1.33pm on November 9 to reports of a casualty on the tracks. Paramedics attended alongside officers but sadly a man was pronounced dead at the scene, the force confirmed on November 10. A British Transport Police spokesperson said: "This incident is not being treated as suspicious and a file will be prepared for the coroner." Train services were severely disrupted yesterday afternoon after the incident. Services run by Thameslink, Lumo, LNER, Great Northern, Hull Trains and Grand Central were affected. Lines reopened by 4pm, but residual disruption continued to affect services running between Peterborough and London.
